By only planting the corals that perform well on these heat tests, you might miss colonies that have other important strengths, such as the ability to withstand disease. In fact, future research may reveal that testing corals for one of these other traits may ultimately be a better predictor of their survival in the era of climate change, says James Guest, a reef ecologist at Newcastle University in England.
Palumbi readily admits that the short picnic cooler tests are not perfect. But the important question, he says, is whether they are good enough — good enough to start using them now to help reefs as the science around fitness testing gradually improves.
That much is clear, he says, and several other researchers I spoke to agreed. While the utility and accuracy of short heat tests is not yet proven, people who want to rebuild reefs should still use them, they said. For restoration, there simply aren’t many better alternatives.
“It’s quick, it’s easy to do, people can apply it relatively straightforwardly, and it offers some kind of test,” Guest told me. “Coming up with these practical approaches makes sense.”
The sun was still low in the sky as Palumbi and I strapped on our tanks and weights and plunged into the ocean near one of Palau’s floating islands.
Sinking down felt like descending onto an alien planet. There were rolling hills of branching coral and stacks of plate coral the size of merry-go-rounds. Schools of colorful fish flew over them, like flocks of birds across a woodland.
Toward the end of the dive, we came across a single coral colony as large as a suburban home. The surface was lumpy and covered in what looked like large bulbous fingers. Given its size, the coral was likely at least three hundred years old.
When we were back on the boat, I asked Palumbi what he thought of the reef. “It doesn’t get better than this,” he said.
Isn’t it arrogant to think we can recreate, or even fortify, something as complex as a coral reef?
There could have been 200 species of coral on this one reef alone, Palumbi said, some of which may still be unknown to science. If this is what coral reefs are supposed to look like, even our best science probably can’t recreate them.
It seems like our time would be far better spent trying to prevent reefs like this from dying in the first place. “We all know that we have to solve the bigger problem,” Guest said. “If we don’t reduce carbon emissions and we don’t deal with climate change, nothing we do is going to help corals.”
But the way Guest and other scientists see it, restoration — and the science to improve it — is not about recreating thriving coral reefs. The goal is much more humble, and much more depressing: to prevent as many species and reefs as possible from disappearing altogether so that, if and when the planet cools back down, there’s still something left to regrow.
Reef restoration encompasses a broad range of approaches, Guest said, meant to “stop species and populations from going off into an extinction vortex.” It would seem anything that might help that cause even a little bit — including a handful of plastic picnic coolers — is worth a try.

How does someone feel lonely while being deeply loved? How does someone feel unsupported while living in a joint family? Despite partners, families and friends, many adults feel nobody truly knows them. As loneliness draws growing global concern, this paradox deserves attention. While technology, urbanisation and changing social structures all play a role, growing evidence suggests that its roots may begin much earlier — in childhood.
The World Health Organization estimates that one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, with significant consequences for health and well-being. The report highlighted that loneliness is linked to around 100 deaths every hour globally.
One of the largest studies ever conducted on loneliness, led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues, and published in Perspectives on Psychological Science in 2015, analysed data from more than 3.4 million participants and found that loneliness was associated with a 26% higher risk of premature mortality. Loneliness has also been linked to heart disease, depression, weakened immunity, disturbed sleep and cognitive decline. These findings tell us why loneliness matters. But they do not explain why two people living in similar circumstances experience relationships so differently.
The India story
In India, we often assume that close-knit families protect against loneliness. However, many adults still feel emotionally isolated despite living with family and appearing socially connected. Young adults are moving away for education and work, traditional neighbourhood networks are weakening, and older adults are increasingly living alone. These changes undoubtedly contribute to loneliness. But they do not explain why many people feel emotionally alone even while surrounded by loved ones. Emotional loneliness often starts within families when people never feel safe enough to reveal who they truly are.
While researching Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and their long-term consequences, one observation repeatedly stood out. Many adults described a quiet, persistent loneliness that had little to do with the number of people in their lives. Childhood adversity is often imagined as dramatic — abuse, violence. Yet much of it leaves no visible mark.
A child who grows up feeling emotionally unseen, criticised rather than comforted, or accepted only when meeting expectations, gradually learns to become invisible, adapting to cope. Some adapt by creating an external persona that appears outgoing and entertaining. These adaptations may help children survive difficult environments, but they can later become barriers to intimacy, trust and genuine connection.
Among ACEs, interpersonal experiences such as emotional neglect and peer isolation may be where adult loneliness begins. Long before adulthood, they shape a child’s expectations of relationships. Children learn to protect themselves by hiding vulnerability. Adults may continue using the same strategy long after the threat has passed.
Our recently published study among Indian adults found that ACEs were strongly linked to lasting difficulties in managing emotions, self-worth and relationships — the kind of struggles often seen in people carrying deep, unresolved trauma. Childhood experiences accounted for nearly half of the variation in these difficulties. This suggests that loneliness is not always a matter of limited social contact; it may also reflect deeper disruptions in the capacity to trust, feel safe and experience belonging. Our findings suggest loneliness extends beyond health, affecting well-being, relationships and quality of life.
This distinction is important to understand since it shapes how we respond. Public health initiatives often encourage people to socialise more, join community groups or spend less time online. These are worthwhile. However, for someone whose nervous system has learnt that closeness feels unpredictable or unsafe, simply increasing social contact may not reduce loneliness.
What emotional safety looks like
By contrast, children who grow up feeling emotionally safe, accepted and supported are more likely to develop a lasting sense of trust and belonging that protects against loneliness later in life. Recovery often begins with relationships in which people no longer feel they must hide who they are.
This is not about blaming parents. Most caregivers do their best with the emotional resources they received. Understanding these patterns is not about assigning guilt. It is about recognising how emotional experiences pass from one generation to the next, and how they can be transformed.
Loneliness affects health, productivity, relationships and healthy ageing. In a country with a large working population under 35, investing in children’s emotional well-being is not only a mental health priority, but also a long-term social and economic investment. As India strengthens its commitment to mental health, recognising the role of early emotional experiences offers an opportunity to invest in prevention, not only treatment. Instead of asking only “Why am I lonely?”, we might also ask, “When did I first learn that I had to face my feelings alone?” For many people, that offers a more compassionate understanding of why connection can feel so difficult.
When a child grows up around adults who stay calm amidst chaos, and who accept and help them navigate difficult emotions, the child feels accepted and confident. For this, adults need to work on their own trauma.
If India is serious about addressing its growing loneliness crisis, the conversation must extend beyond technology and changing lifestyles. To tackle loneliness, we must begin where connection begins: childhood.
The writers are co-authors of What Happened to Me? vs What’s Wrong with Me?: Indian Perspectives on Childhood Trauma and Recovery (Penguin Random House India).

More than one in three older adults surveyed in a Hyderabad-based study showed signs of mild cognitive impairment, with researchers finding a strong association between cognitive decline and deficiencies in several key vitamins.
Micronutrients deficiencies in older adults with mild cognitive impairment
The findings by scientists at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) suggest that better nutritional status may play an important role in preserving brain health as people age. Older adults with mild cognitive impairment were more likely to have deficiencies in several micronutrients, particularly vitamins D, B2 and B9, highlighting the potential role of nutrition in maintaining brain health during ageing.
Published in the international journal ‘Nutrients’, the study - Neuronal Biomarkers and Micronutrient Status in Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment, also identified significant associations between blood levels of essential vitamins, neuronal biomarkers and cognitive performance. The findings underscore the importance of early nutritional assessment and intervention among older adults at risk of cognitive decline.
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is considered an intermediate stage between normal ageing and dementia, in which individuals experience measurable changes in memory and thinking abilities but can still perform their daily activities independently.
What was assessed?
The community-based cross-sectional study involved 184 adults aged 55 to 85 years from the city. Cognitive function was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), while blood samples were analysed for vitamins A, D, B1, B2, B6, B9 and B12. Researchers also measured neuronal biomarkers, including beta-amyloid, total tau, neurofilament light chain and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
Anthropometric measurements, blood pressure, blood glucose levels and other biochemical parameters were also evaluated to identify factors associated with early cognitive impairment. It was found that 36.4% of participants had mild cognitive impairment. The affected individuals had lower blood levels of several micronutrients, including vitamins D, B1, B2, B6, B9 and B12. Deficiencies in vitamins D, B2 and B9 were particularly more prevalent among the MCI group.
Better cognitive performance
Participants with MCI also had significantly higher blood glucose levels and elevated systolic blood pressure. In contrast, higher levels of vitamins, especially vitamins D and B6, were associated with better cognitive performance.
“While further studies and trials are needed to establish causality and assess the impact of nutrient supplementation, these findings underscore the value of early nutritional assessment and timely interventions as part of healthy ageing strategies,” said Scientist & Head of the biochemistry division at ICMR-NIN, G. Bhanuprakash Reddy, who led the research.
“Healthy ageing requires attention not only to disease management but also to nutritional well-being. Our findings highlight the importance of maintaining adequate micronutrient status and strengthening early nutritional assessment among older adults to support cognitive health and promote healthy ageing,” said ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni, in a press release.

New Delhi, Aug 18: Delhi High Court on Tuesday refused to grant default bail to Jasir Bilal Wani alias Danish, one of the accused in the 2025 Red Fort car bomb blast case.
A bench of Justices Prathiba M Singh and Vikas Mahajan dismissed Wani's appeal challenging a March 30 trial court order rejecting his plea seeking default bail.
“It is held that the accused is not entitled after 90 days. The appeal is liable to be dismissed,” the bench said.
An accused becomes entitled to default bail if the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet within the stipulated time.
The NIA arrested Wani, a Kashmiri accused of being an “active co-conspirator”, in November 2025.
The agency has alleged that Jasir provided technical support for carrying out terror attacks by modifying drones and attempting to make rockets.
It has claimed that he worked closely with suicide bomber Umar un Nabi in planning the Red Fort blast.
A Hyundai i20 car exploded near the Red Fort at 6.52 pm on November 10, 2025, killing 15 people and injuring several others.
Nabi was identified as the suicide bomber behind the fatal explosion.

The story so far: Junior doctors across Andhra Pradesh, under the banner of the Andhra Pradesh Junior Doctors’ Association (APJUDA), began a phased strike on August 11, 2026, demanding a stipend revision that has been due since January 1, 2026. What began as a time-bound withdrawal of non-emergency services has since escalated, through repeated rounds of failed talks with the State government, into a withdrawal of emergency services as well from August 17, affecting Intensive Care Units, casualty wards, and labour rooms in government medical colleges and teaching hospitals across the State.
How did the protest begin?
The dispute traces back to Government Order No. 287, issued by the Health, Medical and Family Welfare Department on December 17, 2009, which provides for a biennial revision of junior doctors’ stipends by about 15%, linked to inflation. Revisions followed in 2019 and 2024. The one due from January 1, 2026, did not come through even after seven months, prompting APJUDA to send its first formal communication to the department in July and threaten a strike from August 4. The government sought a week’s time through the Director of Medical Education to negotiate with the Finance Department and the Health Secretary, and the strike was put on hold.
How did talks break down?
With no written assurance forthcoming, APJUDA issued a fresh notice for August 11. A day’s postponement was sought again, this time to hold a two-day meeting at the APIIC Building in Mangalagiri, with representatives from every government medical college asked to attend. At the meeting, the government offered an annual hike of 3% for postgraduate junior doctors and 5% for house surgeons and interns, against APJUDA’s demand for 30%, a figure corroborated independently by both a senior health official and the Indian Medical Association, Andhra Pradesh State (IMA AP State). The official told The Hindu that the department had, since receiving APJUDA’s first communication in July, been studying stipend revision models followed in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. While acknowledging the demand was “justified,” the official described the 30% figure as “abnormal,” and said the government was “exploring all options.”
Doctors have cited two broad justifications for 30%. Andhra Pradesh’s inflation rate of around 5% a year works out to roughly 10% over the two years since the last revision, they say, and the 2026 revision is meant to be a catch-up for that period rather than a purely forward-looking hike. They have also pointed to a sharp rise in workload, including a three-hour increase in outpatient department timings over the past year and the added burden of digitising health records.
What are the other two demands?
APJUDA has also sought strict adherence to National Medical Commission norms in recruiting MSc and PhD holders to clinical faculty posts, saying recent recruitment has exceeded the NMC’s prescribed cap of under 15% for such appointments, and it opposes a proposed increase in the retirement age of doctors from 62 to 65 years, which it says would shrink recruitment opportunities for younger doctors entering government service.
How widespread is the strike?
All 19 government medical colleges in the State are participating, APJUDA said, including six established in the past two years and older institutions such as Andhra Medical College in Visakhapatnam, Guntur Medical College, Siddhartha Medical College in Vijayawada, Kurnool Medical College, and the medical college in Kadapa. The association estimates around 9,000 junior doctors are involved statewide.
How has the strike progressed?
Phase I (August 11): Withdrawal of non-emergency services from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., with emergency and ICU services maintained.
Phase II (August 12 onwards): Complete withdrawal of non-emergency services, extended to 9 a.m.-4 p.m., alongside a voluntary relay hunger strike. Emergency and ICU services continued to be maintained through this phase.
Revised deadline: APJUDA’s original deadline of August 15, 5 p.m., for a written government response was extended to August 16, 5 p.m., as negotiations continued.
Phase III (from August 17, 8 a.m.): With no satisfactory written response received by the revised deadline, APJUDA began withdrawing emergency services as well, including in Intensive Care Units, casualty and labour rooms, while non-emergency services remain suspended.
Has the medical fraternity weighed in beyond APJUDA?
Yes. IMA A.P. State and the IMA Junior Doctors Network, Andhra Pradesh State, urged the government on August 16 to resolve the 15% stipend revision due under G.O. No. 287 since January 1, 2026, which they said was by then more than seven months overdue. IMA leaders were careful to distinguish this from APJUDA’s separate 30% demand, which they asked the government to “sympathetically consider” as well, citing inflation, workload, and stipend disparities with other States. Dr. S. Balaraju, President, IMA AP State, and Dr. Subhas Chandra Bose Moturi, Hon. General Secretary, IMA A.P. State, jointly appealed to the Health Minister to intervene directly and hold immediate talks with APJUDA, warning that prolonged agitation would serve the interests of neither doctors, the government, nor the public.
What has APJUDA said about patient care?
The association maintained emergency and ICU services through Phases I and II, even as postgraduates, many already working 36 to 48 hours a week and, in some cases, up to 90 hours, joined the protest. Dr. Balagam Dinakar Sai Srinivas, General Secretary, APJUDA, said doctors were sacrificing “valuable time, which we joined this profession to spend caring for patients.” Phase III marks a departure from that position. IMA credited junior doctors for their “responsible approach towards patient care” through the earlier phases and appealed to the public to see the agitation as “not directed against patients.”
What happens next?
APJUDA has said it will not agree to further postponement without a written commitment specifying a firm timeline for a Government Order. “As of now, August 16 is the deadline. From August 17, we will also halt emergency services,” Dr. Dinakar said. With that phase now in effect, and both APJUDA and IMA calling for the Chief Minister, Deputy Chief Minister, and Health Minister to intervene directly, the stand-off’s resolution will depend on whether the government moves beyond verbal assurances to a written order.

Canadian icon Jann Arden marries Icelandic author Thordis Elva: 'Wife and wife'
'Good Mother' singer publicly announced Elva as her girlfriend last year
Those who follow Canadian music icon, actor, author and overall delightful human Jann Arden on social media would likely note the dirt road as much as they took in the happy couple posing on it.
"Jann's road," as Arden calls it, is more than a secluded rural stretch near her property in Springbank, Alta., west of Calgary. It's a character in and of itself. It's where she posts video walks and updates, photos of her beloved dogs at various stages in their lives, where she reflected on the heartache and humour of caring for her aging parents, and then grieved them.
Jann's road is also a place of joy, where more recently, the singer has posted smiling photos with her partner, and then fiancée: Icelandic author and digital rights and gender equality advocate Thordis Elva.
So, as many of her followers noted, it was fitting that Arden announced she and Elva had married over the weekend with a photo of the white-clad couple on none other than Jann's road.
"Wife and wife," Arden posted on Instagram Sunday, along with their wedding date: Aug. 15, 2026.
"Well, this is maybe the most joyous #Jannsroad yet!" commented TV host Jessica Allen.
"#Jannsroad has never looked better!" commented TV and radio host Meredith Shaw.
Couple met at writer's retreat
Arden, 64, who is best known for ballads like Insensitive, Good Mother and Could I Be Your Girl, announced her engagement to Elva on Dec. 31, 2025. The couple initially met at a writer's retreat in Iceland, with former Icelandic first lady Eliza Reid as the inadvertent matchmaker.
Reid was one of many notable guests at the wedding, writing on Instagram that she always joked she started the Icelandic writing retreat "so that two people might meet there, fall in love, and then invite me to the wedding. AND IT HAPPENED!"
Several Canadian celebrities and media personalities also posted images and comments from the wedding, including Syrian Canadian novellist Danny Ramadan, actor Dani Kind, talk show host Cynthia Loyst, MLA Janis Irwin and CBC chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault.
American comedian and actress Chelsea Handler was also evidently in attendance.
"WHAT A BEAUTIFUL DAY," Handler commented on Arden's photo.
"So glad you could make it Chelsea. Meant the world to us," Arden replied.
Congratulations also poured in from Canadian singers k.d. Lang and Bif Naked.
Arden posted a second photo Monday showing the couple holding hands in front of a gazebo laden with colourful flowers.
"What a day!" she wrote.
CBC News has reached out to Arden's management team for comment and has not yet heard back.
'Insistent I carry a bouquet'
Elva was voted Iceland's Woman of the Year in 2015 for her work on gender equality, and Person of the Year in 2017 for her part in the #MeToo movement. Elva is also a playwright, and co-author of the non-fiction book South of Forgiveness.
The couple discussed their upcoming wedding in an Aug. 11 episode of Arden's podcast titled Pre-wedding Jitters and Shitters. They joked that Arden was "the groom," but Elva added that Arden would be the one carrying the bridal bouquet.
"She is insistent that I carry a bouquet," Arden said.
Later in the podcast, Arden said she thought same-sex love should be as normalized as "a sandwich."
"The one thing that I'm very proud of is how much we're just normalizing this.… Normalizing people being in loving relationships and normalizing how society is structured and that we need to do a lot better for all people," Arden said.
"We're both in positions of privilege.... we have power, we have access to media. We're not fu--ing taking any prisoners with us. We don't tolerate it."
They're planning a honeymoon in Edinburgh, Arden said in a previous episode.

Rishabh Pant on Tuesday hit a half-century in the second innings against Sri Lanka in the first match in Galle, and in process completed 100 sixes in Test cricket.
He completed the haul in just his 89th innings, making him the fastest batter to achieve the feat. He is the first Indian and the fourth overall to record this achievement.
Ben Stokes (138), Brendan McCullum (107), Adam Gilchrist (100) are the only others to have achieved it before Pant. Gilchrist was the previous-fastest to 100 sixes in 130 innings, while Stokes and McCullum got to the three-figure mark in 151 and 170 innings, respectively.
For India, the previous best belonged to Virender Sehwag, who had accumulated 91 sixes through his 104-match career.

‘Do as I say, not as I do’ Trump votes by mail after calling it a fraud
Trump pushes Supreme Court to implement sweeping mail-in ballot restrictions even as he participates in Florida primary elections remotely
Donald Trump once again voted by mail in Florida elections despite repeatedly attacking mail-in ballots as “mail-in cheating” and a “scam” that his administration has spent months trying to restrict for millions of Americans.
Records in Palm Beach County, where the president’s primary Mar-a-Lago residence is located, indicate that he requested a mail-in ballot last month to participate in Florida’s Republican primary elections. His ballot was received August 14. Politico first reported his ballot.
Trump has not returned to the Sunshine State since May. He last voted by mail during a special election in March.
But his latest absentee vote follows his administration’s emergency request to the Supreme Court to implement sweeping restrictions on Americans’ access to mail-in ballots, a move that has been repeatedly blocked in court while the president pushes Congress to enact his far-reaching election reform legislation.
“As President Trump has said, the SAVE America Act has commonsense exceptions for Americans to use mail-in ballots for illness, disability, military, or travel – but universal mail-in voting should not be allowed because it’s highly susceptible to fraud,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in a statement shared with The Independent.
“As everyone knows, the President is a resident of Palm Beach and participates in Florida elections, but he obviously primarily lives at the White House in Washington, D.C.,” she said. “This is a non-story.”
Days after casting his ballot by mail in March, Trump described the process as “cheating” during an event in Tennessee.
“Mail-in voting means mail-in cheating. I call it mail-in cheating, and we got to do something about it all,” he said at the time.
During a July speech, he called mail-in ballots “inherently corrupt.” He used February’s State of the Union Address to demand “no more crooked mail-in ballots.”
In 2024, Trump’s presidential campaign and the Republican National Committee launched “Swamp the Vote” to make up for lost ground on mail-in voting among Republican voters in the aftermath of 2020 elections.
“You need to make a plan, register, and vote any way possible,” Trump said in a statement announcing the plan. Days later, Trump told a crowd at the far-right Turning Point Action conference that early voting is “sad” and “crazy.”
“They start early. You know, it’s sad, when you have to go months early,” he said at the time. “It’s crazy. What are they doing with all these votes? What are they doing?”
“Mail-in voting is totally corrupt,” he told supporters at a rally in Michigan in February that year. “Get that through your head.”
Last week, the Trump administration pressed the Supreme Court for permission to implement new rules that could significantly restrict voters’ access to ballots in midterm elections this fall.
Federal courts have blocked the U.S. Postal Service from further implementing Trump’s executive order that sought to create a national voter registration list that would be used to decide who is eligible to cast a ballot.
If the Supreme Court doesn’t stop them, the judge’s rulings will “effectively run out the clock” on the administration’s attempts to implement the executive order before November’s elections, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the high court last week.
Nearly two dozen Democratic-led states, dozens of election officials and more than 50 former state and federal judges have warned the nation’s high court that Trump’s order would create “chaos” for voters and their ballots.
If the justices let the order take effect, “the result will be chaos,” according to a bipartisan coalition of 118 current and former election officials tasked with running the nation’s elections.
Election workers are now in the “untenable position” of carrying out Trump’s order “on pain of threats of criminal prosecution” with elections already underway in most states, forced to overhaul their election systems just weeks before ballots are sent, they said.
Critics fear the president’s efforts to centralize control over election administration, which is left to the states, is an attempt to boost Republican candidates and suppress Democratic turnout ahead of November elections that could determine the balance of power in Congress — and the fate of Trump’s remaining years in office.
Florida voters will select nominees Tuesday to replace term-limited Republican Governor Ron DeSantis.
Eleven GOP candidates are competing for the nomination, including Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, Rep. Byron Donalds, former investment firm CEO James Fishback and former state House Speaker Paul Renner.
The state also will hold its first congressional primaries since adopting a newly redrawn map designed to boost Republican candidates.
Voters also will cast their ballots in a special primary election to fill the Senate seat vacated by now Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Republican Ashley Moody, who is currently filling the seat, is facing two primary challengers, while two candidates are competing for the Democratic nomination.

German court convicts Ukrainian man over Russian sabotage plot
The plot involved posting test packages containing GPS trackers in March last year to Ukraine
A German court on Tuesday handed a jail sentence of one year and three months to a Ukrainian man for spying for Russia and helping prepare possible acts of sabotage.
The court in Stuttgart acquitted two other Ukrainian men aged 22 and 25 who were on trial for the same plot, which involved posting test packages containing GPS trackers in March last year to Ukraine.
The plan was aimed at scoping out possibilities for “disrupting transport and infrastructure” and was ultimately directed by a “Russian state entity”, the court said.
Yevhen Bezchasnyi, 30, was arrested in Switzerland in May 2025 before being extradited to Germany in December.
He was found guilty of “spying for the purposes of sabotage”.
However, the time he has already spent in pre-trial detention counted towards his sentence and he will now be released.

It’s the depths of summer. It’s still stultifyingly, dangerously hot. Going outside is a fool’s game unless you have 500 SPF sunblock and a personal AC unit. Be sensible: Stay inside and enjoy some of the best movies currently streaming instead.
August’s offerings include the return of Avatar: The Last Airbender on Paramount+, with a brand new adventure returning to the cast of the fan-favorite animated series as adults and struggling with newfound responsibilities. The same theme carries over to Heartstopper Forever on Netflix, where teen romance is dashed against the rocks of looming adulthood.
Elsewhere, there’s a double helping of liminal space creepiness from Japan, with the exceptional live action horror Exit 8 on Shudder, and the action epic Demon Slayer The Movie: Infinity Castle—one of the most successful animated movies in Japanese history—on Crunchyroll. And, if you’d rather not have to think in this heat, enjoy an action-packed pairing of Mortal Kombat 2 and Masters of the Universe, two films that aren’t so much “so bad they’re good”, as they are “turn brain off now for fun time.”
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender
Water. Earth. Fire. Air. Only the Avatar is master of all four elements—but Aang, the latest inheritor of the mantle, vanished when he was most needed. Frozen in suspended animation for decades, Aang was awakened by waterbender Katara and her warrior brother Sokka. Joined by earthbender Toph, and firebending enemy-turned-ally Zuko, Team Avatar went on to save the world. Now, as adults, they face an even more daunting task: rebuilding it. Yet with Aang the last living airbender, the world remains out of balance—until he discovers Tagah, an ancient airbender suspended as he once was. No longer alone, the group set out to find an ancient artifact belonging to a forgotten Avatar, in the hope it can restore airbending to the world. But why was Tagah frozen centuries ago, and can he be trusted now?
A direct sequel to the brilliant and beloved 2005 Nickelodeon animated series, this feature length adventure is a more mature outing, growing up with its original audience, and delivering some of the most breathtaking animation you’ll see all year. Sadly robbed of a wide theatrical release—and victim of a notorious leak of the full film—Avatar Aang still shines on the small screen.
Heartstopper Forever
One of the most successful comic book adaptations in years, Alice Oseman’s Heartstopper reaches its long-awaited conclusion with a final movie. Fans have followed the love story of Nick (Kit Connor) and Charlie (Joe Locke) through high school, battling early doubts, coming-out confusion, and mental health struggles along the way. Yet as Nick embarks for university, the pair are forced to ask whether their relationship can survive—especially when friends Elle (Yasmin Finney) and Tao (William Gao) are choosing to break up after graduation. A beautiful ode to young love and queer joy, Heartstopper Forever fizzes with emotion. Grab tissues.
Mortal Kombat II
It’s not big (only $129 million at the box office) and it’s not clever (superpowered martial artists stave off an interdimensional invasion via the fine diplomatic art of punching) but Mortal Kombat II is a hell of a lot of fun. Picking up from the stinger of 2021’s cinematic reboot of the long-running fighting game series, the focus switches to washed-up action movie star Johnny Cage (Karl Urban), who must prove he has what it takes to stand as one of Earthrealm’s defenders. Diving into some of the weirder fantasy elements of the source material, director Simon McQuoid delivers some incredible action set pieces, with fight scenes that deliver all the brutality fans expect, and a surprisingly sharp comedic edge throughout.
Masters of the Universe
When his home of Eternia was invaded, Prince Adam (Nicholas Galatzine) was sent to Earth for his own protection. Now, he’s a weirdo stuck in a dead-end corporate job who won’t stop talking about the fantasy world he came from—until his old friend Teela (Camila Mendes) tracks him down to take him home and fight off the forces of Skeletor.
As yet another go at bringing the 40-plus-year-old toyline-slash-cartoon advert for the toy line to the big screen, Masters of the Universe was probably doomed from the start. Yet director Travis Knight (Bumblebee, aka the only good live action Transformers movie) completely understood the assignment, delivering a wildly imaginative, colorful, and just-the-right-level-of-stupid adventure that embraces and pokes fun at its source material in equal measure. It’s charming, funny—shout out to Idris Elba as drunken, derelict mentor Man-at-Arms and Kristen Wiig as the voice of sardonic robot Roboto—and undeniably camp, and should tickle older fans’ nostalgia centers as much as it entertains their own little warriors.
Exit 8
A lost man (Kazunari Ninomiya) wanders through the stark white corridors of Tokyo’s subway system, searching for Exit 8. He’s trapped, not because of the labyrinthine layout of one of the world’s busiest transit systems, but because any wrong move sends him back to Exit 0. The only way out is to avoid “anomalies,” which may be as subtle as a changed poster in the looping tunnels, or blood flooding down from the ceiling—and each loop, the anomalies change, making escape feel maddeningly impossible.
Director Genki Kawamura brings the cult indie video game to life in this masterful slice of Japanese horror cinema, expanding on its claustrophobic sense of dread with a much-needed exploration of who the Lost Man is and why he’s caught in the unsettling liminal underworld. If you’re a fan of Backrooms, you owe it to yourself to watch Exit 8.
Spider-Man MCU Trilogy
With Spider-Man: Brand New Day riding high in theaters, it’s the perfect time to dive back into Tom Holland’s first quasi-trilogy as the webbed wonder. After debuting in Civil War (also on Disney+), Holland’s Peter Parker establishes his heroic bona fides facing the Vulture (Michael Keaton) in Homecoming, goes on a world tour and fights Mysterio (Jake Gyllenhaal) in Far From Home, and battles a multiverse of menaces in No Way Home—luckily with some assistance from previous cinematic Spider-Men Peter Parker (Tobey Maguire) and Peter Parker (Andrew Garfield). The real success of Holland’s films isn’t in the superpowered theatricality, but the way they bring Peter’s messy personal life straight from the comics to the screen, focusing as much on his supporting cast—chiefly love interest MJ (Zendaya), best friend Ned (Jacob Batalon), and Aunt May (Marisa Tomei)—as on his superheroic adventures.
The Blackening
When a group of Black college friends hold a reunion for Juneteenth, the vibe seems off. They’re meeting at a cabin in the woods for a start, which is a little too close to horror movie territory for anyone’s liking. Such genre-savviness begins to pay off when they discover a suspicious board game in the basement and find themselves playing by a serial killer’s twisted rules—starting with determining the “Blackest” member of the group to sacrifice.
With a cast of comedy greats including X Mayo, Jermaine Fowler, and Jay Pharoah, The Blackening is a self-aware and smartly satirical twist on horror movie conventions that brilliantly plays on its tongue-in-cheek tagline, “We can’t all die first.”
Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba—Infinity Castle
Based on the manga by Koyoharu Gotouge, Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba is set in an alternate Taishō era Japan where a corps of specially trained warriors hunt down ferocious demons. Infinity Castle follows on directly from the fourth season of the television anime series, which is also on Crunchyroll for anyone who cares to do the homework, but this full-length movie is a thrill ride even if you’re jumping in blind.
After narrowly surviving an attack by the Demon Slayers, Muzan—progenitor demon and all-around big bad—traps the heroes in his stronghold, the ever-shifting dimensional prison of the Infinity Castle. Cue one epic battle royale as the Demon Slayer Corps fights their way to freedom, navigating the unpredictable landscape and seeing off scores of powerful foes—including a rematch between series lead Tanjiro Kamado (Natsuki Hanae in Japanese, Zach Aguilar in English) and powerful demon rival Akaza. The first in a planned trilogy set to cap the entire Demon Slayer saga, Infinity Castle is a visually stunning supernatural adventure.
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
Set decades after 2017’s War for the Planet of the Apes (but still a long way out from Charlton Heston screaming at the Statue of Liberty in the 1968 original), Kingdom opens with society’s tables having fully turned. Evolved apes rule, while most humans have been reduced to feral, nonverbal states. When Noa (Owen Teague), a young falconer from a chimpanzee clan, encounters an unusually intelligent human, Mae (Freya Allen), the unlikely pair are drawn into the orbit of Proximus Caesar (Kevin Durand), a power-hungry ape-king aiming to open a lost vault of human technology.
While it all leads to an unusually explosive conflict for a world that’s reverted to blood and bone barbarism, the film packs in a surprisingly deep examination of humanity’s relationship with the world around us. It’s also the best the series has ever looked, with incredible effects work and striking location shoots in Australia creating a fully believable post-apocalyptic world. Newly arrived on Prime Video, Kingdom may be the fourth installment in the Planet of the Apes reboot-prequel series, but as a standalone entry, it makes for a strong entry point.

CWC meet to chart expansion of Rahul’s ‘Chhatron ki Goonj’
Rahul Gandhi's 'Chhatron ki Goonj' outreach program aims to engage students post-protests, focusing on education reforms and issues affecting youth.
The Congress Working Committee (CWC) is expected to chalk out a strategy on Wednesday to “expand the scope” of Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi’s popular programme ‘Chhatron ki Goonj’, which started from Kota to interact with students. The next episode is planned at Pune.
According to a senior strategist of the party, the upcoming CWC meeting will also discuss the party’s preparations for the upcoming elections in Uttar Pradesh and Punjab.
As the Congress leadership finalises the meeting’s agenda, party strategists said expanding Chhatron ki Gunj is high on the agenda. “We must expand the programme and keep the momentum alive,” said a leader. The outreach programme is an interactive convention to discuss education reforms, jobs and other student-related issues.
Also Read | Rahul raising students’ voice through ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’: Congress’s UP in-charge
Starting on June 17, Gandhi’s student outreach programme has been held at Kota, Dehradun and Prayagraj. The fourth edition, exclusively for female students, will be held in Pune on August 22. “India’s girls deserve a future without barriers. Raise your voice and be part of the movement,” Congress said on X on Monday.
A portal launched by the party to attract students has already got 2.5 million members with more than 91,000 WhatsApp members. According to the portal, the membership is active across 28 cities.
Gandhi had earlier described the student protest as “not anger, not violence, not hatred. This was a deep expression of the youth of this country, of the future generation of this country.”
“The programme is important to the Congress as it is an outreach effort to the students and the Gen Z in the wake of the student protests in central Delhi and other parts of India that led to the resignation of (then) education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and forced the government to take a series of steps,” a second leader said. Prime Minister Narendra Modi formed a six-member task force led by former UIDAI chief Nandan Nilekani while the NTA sacked 50 staff members to reform the exam system.
Now, Gandhi’s outreach to students assumes greater importance after The National Testing Agency (NTA) on Sunday accounted re-conduct of the University Grants Commission National Eligibility Test (UGC-NET) examination for three papers, after “multiple errors” were found in the exam conducted from June 22 to June 30 this year.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

When Jim Allen, the elections director for Delaware County, Pennsylvania, recently ran a training session for poll workers, he began a conversation about a topic he’d never previously had to address during training: prediction markets. “There was one person who stood up, and they said, ‘Well, what if we just want to make a minor bet on what turnout will be, that'll keep things interesting?’ And we said: ‘No, this is all bad,’” Allen, who oversees 383 precincts, recounts.
As a result, Allen and the board of elections in Delaware County amended the oaths signed by people involved in elections to include “an affirmation that the workers have no direct or indirect interests in any bets, wagers, or prediction markets.”
Some 2,500 people, including everyone from full-time staff in the elections office to temporary employees helping process ballots on Election Day, have signed the oath ahead of November’s midterms.
“The rapid growth of prediction markets, and their plans to prey on elections, are direct threats to undermining trust in electoral outcomes,” Allen tells WIRED. “The overriding concern is that prediction markets have the potential to monetize a reward for manipulating results and, equally concerning, capitalizing on the anger and frustration by those who lose in these prediction markets.”
Increased Threats
With less than 100 days left until the midterms, and with President Donald Trump and members of his administration working overtime to undermine trust in American democracy, WIRED spoke to election officials across the country struggling to get their heads around how prediction markets could further complicate Election Day. Last week’s Wisconsin gubernatorial primary showcased how large the discrepancy can be between prediction market odds and how a race actually shakes out, as both Kalshi and Polymarket had progressive candidate Francesca Hong as the likely winner until the results started coming in. (Traditional polling was also wildly off.) Election officials see risk in this type of scenario, where people place too much confidence in the probabilities shown by the markets and make wagers expecting guaranteed money. There’s also concern over whether prediction markets could fuel aggression against poll workers and other people involved in elections, something that some officials say they’ve already witnessed.
Prediction markets “fed a lot of the volatility in the aftermath of the June election,” says Dean Logan, county clerk for Los Angeles County, the country’s most populous election jurisdiction, during a webinar organized by the Partnership for Large Election Jurisdictions. “I won't go into great detail about how that resulted in threats or aggressiveness from observers or people who had a stake in the outcome of the election, but it is something that we definitely saw, and we saw it at a level that we haven't seen in prior elections.”
“Let us be unambiguous: Threatening an election official or poll worker is a crime, and Kalshi condemns it in the strongest terms, full stop,” Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick says.
Both Kalshi and Polymarket tell WIRED that they will not allow markets about whether there will be unrest at the polls.
One of the concerns election officials repeatedly raised was that voters appear to be confused about just what the odds in election markets represent. This was backed up by a recent survey conducted by the Partnership for Large Election Jurisdictions, which found that 75 percent of respondents were unable to correctly say what prediction market odds represented, with 35 percent of respondents claiming they were either counted votes or official projections from state officials.
“Prediction markets are a form of speculation, but they are increasingly being presented, and in some cases interpreted, as indicators of likely election outcomes,” Logan tells WIRED. “The challenge is that many people don't distinguish between a market reflecting the views of participants and the official election process.”
For years, election deniers have leveraged the fact that many election processes are not very well understood by the general public to push disinformation. Now, officials are concerned that misunderstanding what predictions markets represent will make that situation even worse.
“What happens when there's a difference between what the prediction markets show and what the certified results show?” Amy Cohen, executive director of the National Association of State Election Directors, tells WIRED. “That's hard, because you're combining two topics that the general public doesn't have a great understanding of, which is elections and prediction markets."
While election officials consider how to address these issues, prominent prediction market trader Caleb Davies sees some fears over market integrity as overblown. “They sound like valid concerns, but I just don't think that they hold up to much scrutiny,” he says. If somebody attempts to manipulate a race by spiking the odds in favor of an underdog, there will be politics traders monitoring the market who see an opportunity to make money correcting it. “A smart trader is going to see that and then drive them right back to being an underdog almost immediately and just make the profits from it—it’s not a wise strategy.”
Polymarket spokesperson Annabel Walsh made a similar point. “Other traders will recognize that there's an opportunity to turn a profit off of that artificial boost,” she says. There are recent examples of how this type of market will quickly correct when a trader appears to attempt to skew the results, and when asked about this risk, Kalshi sent WIRED a case study it published on an event during the Los Angeles mayoral election. In that incident, someone on Kalshi placed an enormous bet on Spencer Pratt winning that was notably out of step with how he was polling; it skewed the odds for 9 seconds.
Still, concerns remain that manipulation is possible, especially in races with fewer participants speculating on the outcome than something like the closely watched LA race. Some House races currently have only a few thousand dollars wagered, which means it does not take much money to impact odds. Andrew Cates, a Texas-based election law attorney, worries that smaller election markets with low volume can be easily manipulated: “Anybody could place a big bet on a race and skew at least the perception of the odds of that person winning, and the overall groundswell of support for that person.”
Insider Trading
Betting on the outcome of elections on prediction markets was a niche pursuit for many years. The smaller prediction market platform PredictIt has offered election trading since 2014 and continues to operate. Notably, it has stricter guardrails than newer competitors and lets people trade only as much as $3,500 on each race. “Unlike Kalshi and Polymarket, PredictIt caps individual positions,” PredictIt public relations director Toni Galeassi tells WIRED. “As prediction markets grow, we believe responsible market design, including appropriate limits and clear communication about what market probabilities represent are important.” Galeassi also called any threats to election workers “unacceptable.”
In 2024, Fortune reported that $3.2 billion had been wagered on the outcome of the presidential election. One French user of Polymarket won $80 million after predicting that Donald Trump would win. But companies like Kalshi and Polymarket have seen massive growth in recent months and are poised to go even more mainstream. “This is our first real, full election cycle for national elections where prediction markets have been fully unleashed,” says Amanda Fischer, a former SEC official who now directs policy for the financial reform nonprofit Better Markets. Both Kalshi and Polymarket have dedicated midterm hubs on their platforms.
The increased interest was seen in California in June, during the primary for the Los Angeles mayoral race, when affiliate marketers paid by Kalshi and Polymarket paid right-wing influencers to post content questioning the outcome of the vote. The companies’ rules prohibit affiliates from posting election-denial content; after public outcry, they made the influencers remove the “paid promotion” tags on their posts, and both companies tell WIRED that they will ask affiliates to comply with their guidelines. But it’s an open question as to whether some of these affiliates will continue to spew false narratives about elections. “Those accounts can influence narratives and voter behavior,” notes Fischer.
There have been multiple prosecutions of insider trading on prediction markets, and election officials are concerned about this happening on Election Day given that some election officials are aware of the final results before they become public. “Prediction markets lead to possible manipulation or even insider trading,” Jared DeMarinis, administrator of elections for the Maryland State Board of Elections, tells WIRED. “The threat grows as these sites become increasingly popular and legitimatized by the media in lieu of polling. Just like in cases of election disinformation, once it takes root it will take Herculean efforts to undo its damage to the electoral process.”
DeMarinis revealed to WIRED that his office was also looking to follow Delaware County’s lead and demand that those involved in running elections in the state sign a declaration that they are not going to use prediction markets to bet on the outcome of the election. And they are not the only ones. In July, Arizona Secretary of State Andrian Fontes banned his staff from using nonpublic information to place bets on elections on prediction markets.
“We are reinforcing our internal policies to ensure that non-public information, particularly information related to election administration, is never used or shared by staff for personal gain or unauthorized purposes,” Monica Gordon, Cook County clerk, tells WIRED.
Surveillance
As well as demanding election workers sign oaths, some states are making it explicit just what punishments await for those who bet on elections. Last month, the Wisconsin Elections Commission warned voters they "cannot, even indirectly, make a bet or wager on the outcome of an election and then vote in that same election." A Kalshi employee on X described the move as “active voter suppression.”
It’s already against the law to trade on inside information on prediction markets, and a variety of state authorities have attempted to enact a patchwork of laws explicitly forbidding government employees from doing so. The platforms also have internal rules. “Specifically in elections, we have a broad list of people that are not allowed to be in the markets, where if you're a donor, a staffer, a family member of staffers, and many more, you’re not allowed in the markets,” Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such says. In the past year, Kalshi has flagged a number of market manipulation and insider trading cases to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, including a Senate candidate who later claimed he bet on himself deliberately.
Another Kalshi spokesperson, Jacki McGavick, emphasized that the company “aggressively surveils” election markets. “We have developed surveillance software that preemptively blocks certain prohibited traders—rather than just enforcing retroactively—for all political markets,” she tells WIRED.
Polymarket recently hired former FBI official Shana Bautista, who also worked at Coinbase, as its global head of investigations and intelligence. The company says it cannot share specifics of active investigations but that it has increased the size of the team monitoring elections in advance of the midterms. “When it comes to elections, and how sensitive they are, our team of investigators is actively reviewing and identifying anomalous activity, and then we have robust and standard processes for handling it,” Bautista says.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees prediction markets at the federal level, has no plans to do any midterm-specific market integrity surveillance. “The CFTC is extensively monitoring election markets, just like all other markets, for manipulation, fraud, or insider trading,” spokesperson Brooke Nethercott tells WIRED.
Some prediction market critics believe that laws need to be changed to take this much further, to prevent government officials from participating altogether as a guardrail against manipulation and potential corruption. “All federal government employees at any level, any part of the federal government, and the military, should be banned from using prediction markets at all,” says Alexandra Thornton, the senior director for financial regulation at the Center for American Progress. “It should be sort of a condition of employment.”

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.
The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.
For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.
The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.
Anshika Pandey, 20, Delhi
Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.
Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.
This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.
“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.
Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.
Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.
Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.
Sufi Shaheen, 19, Delhi
Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.
Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.
It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.
“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.
Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.
A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.
When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.
“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.
Pradeep Kumar Mahich, 22, Rajasthan
“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.
No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.
“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.
“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.
On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.
Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.
S Anitha, 17, Tamil Nadu
S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.
As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”
She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.
Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.
When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.
Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.
He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

Petlibro founder and CEO York Wu provided more information about an outage that left users unable to control their smart pet feeders through the companion app and, in some reported cases, left them with hungry pets.
Petlibro, a company owned by Shenzhen, China-headquartered firm Shenzhen Libro Technology Co., first acknowledged the outage on Tuesday at 5 am PT. At 7 pm PT on Wednesday, Petlibro said the outage was resolved. Notably, some people online reported different information at the time, and some claimed to still have problems as of August 13.
In a blog post on Saturday that included an apology and acknowledgement of the “frustration and concern” the outage caused, Wu confirmed that problems with Petlibro’s cloud server caused the outage:
The outage was due to cloud server issues that caused a backlog of data requests, overloading the system memory and bringing down device service in the process. After successfully restarting the cloud service, the backlog reoccurred and the system went down again. At that point, the team conducted systematic troubleshooting of the cloud service system, identified the underlying issue, patched a solution, and then closely monitored the slow upscale of traffic towards stable recovery.
Because of this outage, the app was no longer able to connect to devices and as a result device communication was not possible. Services related to the app, including on-demand actions, operation history, records, notifications, and videos, were unavailable.
Wu noted that Petlibro has “increased demand capacity” and is “preparing an audit protocol to search our backend and work to resolve any similar inconsistencies.”
Outage timeline
Wu said that at 5:20 am PT on Tuesday, August 11, a “critical error occurred affecting app login and control.” At 6:20 am PT, “app functionality was restored, and the system began to process a large backlog of data requests resulting from the outage.” But 23 minutes later, “a flood of incoming requests overwhelmed connection capacity, and the system failed again,” per Wu.
At 8:04 am PT “basic functionality was restored,” and Petlibro started restoring other services, Wu said. About an hour later, “the app’s loading time slowed,” so Petlibro decided to “scale back functionality,” the exec said.

Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang scored on debut but Deportivo La Coruna was held to a 1-1 home draw by Elche as it returned to La Liga after an eight-year absence on Monday.
Deportivo is back in the top flight for the first time since being relegated, with Clarence Seedorf as coach, in 2017-18.
The 1999-00 La Liga champion, which also reached two Champions League quarterfinals and one semifinal in the early 2000s, has also since spent four seasons languishing in the third tier.
It was promoted last term as La Liga 2 runner-up.

Aubameyang scored Deportivo’s first goal back in fine style midway through the opening half, killing fellow new signing Lorenzo Amatucci’s long ball over the top with a magnificent touch before drilling a left-footed strike into the bottom corner.

Deportivo could not hang on for victory, though, as Marc Aguado’s 76th-minute header grabbed Elche a point.

The best AI tools for job interview preparation include Exponent Practice, AceRound AI, Yoodli, MyInterviewAI, Interviewing.io, Big Interview, Huru AI, and Ophy AI. They offer mock interviews, role-specific questions, resume-based practice, technical prep, and detailed feedback.
AI has already changed how companies hire, right from resume shortlisting and initial assessments to interview screening. Thankfully, the same technology can also work in your favor. AI tools for job interview preparation can help you understand a role, research the company, prepare likely questions, practice mock interviews, and even point out where your answers fall short.
While mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are more than capable of helping with the basics, dedicated AI interview tools take things a step further. We tested eight such tools that offer everything from resume-based interview questions and technical interview practice to video analysis, peer interviews, and detailed feedback. Here is how they work, which one you should choose, and how to get the most out of them.
If you want to skip directly to the best AI Tools use the Table of Contents below.
Table of Contents
How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.

You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.
