The government’s controversial NDIS bill will undergo “substantial” amendments after Labor and the Coalition struck a deal, with some of the changes attracting heavy criticism from the Greens, the ACT senator David Pocock and the disability community.
Sixty-three government amendments across both houses will be introduced as part of backroom deals to pass the bill on Tuesday night, the NDIS ministers, Mark Butler and Jenny McAllister, revealed.
Butler said some changes are “relatively technical” while others are “relatively substantial”.
“They will ensure that this bill is the best version it can be,” the minister said.
The bill will go to a vote in the Senate at 8pm where it’s expected to pass with the Coalition’s support.
Among them is a tweak to allow vulnerable participants whose budget is impacted by a new ministerial power – which allows the minister to bluntly slash funding from certain categories across all participants by up to 99% – to apply for more funding through a plan variation.
“We do recognise that there is a need to safeguard against risk to participate in health and safety, particularly for that group of people who require support 24 hours a day,” McAllister said.
“And so we are establishing a new plan variation pathway for people who have high support needs. This is intended to address participants who require continuous care over a 24-hour period. These participants will be able to apply for a plan variation within 90 days of a support determination applying to them.”
The ministerial power to swiftly reduce funding for support categories across all participants has been heavily criticised by both the Greens and ACT senator, David Pocock, as well as the disability community.
In a Tuesday evening debate, Pocock said the change remained the biggest “red line” for him in supporting the bill, describing it as an “indiscriminate cut” impacting hundreds of thousands of participants.
“[In the Senate inquiry], we heard that this will leave people in unsafe situations because it risks isolating them. We know that isolation increases the risks of violence, abuse, and exploitation, and social and community participation is an essential safeguard against this,” Pocock said.
“The indiscriminate nature of this cut means that we will not know its impact until harm happens, and I can’t support that based on what I’ve heard from Canberrans.
“That is something that I cannot support, even though I support the intent of these reforms, minister.”
Steele-John said the changes would impact people with disabilities who require support workers to go into the community.
“This government, in this bill, will be cutting the supports currently available, currently funded, to enable a disabled person to go outside, maybe once or twice a week,” he said.
“The ripple effects of this will be terrible. The stress that it will create is beyond imagining.”
The government estimates the $52bn-a-year scheme will have more than doubled in cost in a decade’s time without intervention. The changes within the bill are expected to instead improve the federal budget’s bottom line by $37.8bn over four years.
McAllister said the government was concerned the fast-rising costs would negatively impact broad support within Australia for the NDIS.
“I don’t think that the community broadly believes that a scheme that costs $100bn a year by the middle of next decade is a scheme that is operating sustainably,” she said.
“But that is the path that we are on, unless sensible amendments are made to the operation of the scheme to ensure that [the NDIS] works as intended.”
The government’s amendment does not exempt any participant from being impacted by the broad funding reductions but it gives those with high support needs a chance to remedy any sudden financial shortfalls from the change.
The Coalition also secured amendments to create new criminal and civil penalties against anyone offering or providing kickbacks using NDIS funding.
Aggravated integrity offences, including obtaining funds by deception, providing false or misleading information, intentionally destroying records and abuse of position as a participant’s nominee will also be introduced.
The government’s plan to pass the NDIS changes this week were almost postponed by the Coalition’s ultimatum to bring tax law changes to close the “widow tax” loophole early.
It was expected that the tax reforms, which include closing the loophole, will be voted on Wednesday morning.

This summer camp kept an instructor who pleaded guilty to assaulting kids. Ontario law allows it
At a Kawartha Lakes camp, a cop who pleaded guilty to assaulting kids kept working there for weeks this summer
KL Hockey in Kawartha Lakes, which offers day and overnight programming for children in July and August, aims “to bring the best to campers everyday — on and off the ice,” its website reads.
But for weeks this summer, one of its lead instructors was a man who recently pleaded guilty to charges of assaulting children.
Bradley Gibbs, who is a Durham Regional Police officer, pleaded guilty in April to two charges of assaulting children who were known to him, his lawyer confirmed. CBC News cannot provide further details due to a court publication ban.
Gibbs is currently described on the camp’s website as “an active coach and mentor to many in the Kawartha Lakes region.” However, he chose to step down on Wednesday afternoon, according to an email that was sent to the camp's parents one day after CBC News contacted Gibbs and the camp for this story.
- Former Durham cop charged in 2nd historic sexual assault, several other charges dropped
- Durham deputy chief retires after misconduct finding over 'racially inappropriate term'
Camp leadership told parents in the email they have supported Gibbs as he dealt with a personal legal matter over the past year. But they did not say whether they knew about the guilty pleas, or why he was allowed to stay on despite them.
There is currently no Ontario legislation that requires summer camps to screen staff that work with children. Camps are not required to get criminal record checks or more extensive vulnerable sector checks from their employees.
The Ontario Camps Association (OCA) requires its 400-plus accredited members to vet staff with criminal record checks. But membership in the non-profit organization is voluntary, meaning summer camps that aren’t part of the OCA — including KL Hockey Camp — don’t have to meet any standards when it comes to vetting staff.
The camp’s director Amanda Tayles said in a statement that Gibbs “has publicly taken accountability for his personal actions.”
“Our focus remains entirely on maintaining a safe, supportive, and positive environment for our summer camp players,” she wrote.
CBC News reached out to Gibbs for comment, but he did not respond before deadline. He is expected to appear in court in September for sentencing.
Gibbs is still employed at Durham Regional Police Services, where he’s currently redeployed from frontline patrol duties to an administrative role, a police spokesperson said. Any potential internal disciplinary proceedings will be informed partly “by the outcome of the ongoing criminal matter, including the sentencing,” Const. Nicholas Gluckstein said in an email.
‘Big gap’ in Ontario legislation for summer camps: lawyer
One of Gibbs’ victims, who is now an adult, spoke with CBC News before Gibbs announced his departure.
“If I had sent my kid to [KL Hockey], I’d be really concerned,” said the victim, whose identity is protected under the court publication ban.
They said Gibbs co-founded the camp with his friends and that camp leadership are aware of the guilty pleas. CBC News has asked the camp if leadership knew about Gibbs’ pleas, but they did not directly respond to the question.
The lack of legislated requirements for summer camps is a “big gap,” said Puneet Tiwari, an employment litigator and partner at Levitt LLP in Toronto.
He said the province should consider legislation that requires summer camps to get vulnerable sector checks from their employees.
Vulnerable sector checks are for people who intend to work with groups considered vulnerable, such as children.
According to the province’s website, they include the same information as a criminal record check, but may also have additional details on outstanding charges, arrest warrants, absolute and conditional discharges and information about charges that didn’t result in a conviction.
The Durham Regional Police Service website provides examples of who might require vulnerable sector checks, which include coaches and parent volunteers for sports or school trips.
CBC News asked the Ministry of the Solicitor General whether the province would consider creating legislation that requires summer camps to get vulnerable sector checks from their employees, but did not receive a response.
The Ministry of Education does require “day camps” for children under four to get a child-care license and make their staff complete a vulnerable sector check, according to its website. But camps for children over the age of four aren’t considered child-care centres, and don’t fall under the ministry’s scope.
The Ministry of Education declined to comment for this story.
Still, Tiwari said it's common sense for camps to require vulnerable sector checks when they’ve been entrusted with children, regardless of the law.
“[Camps] bear the responsibility to screen, supervise and act on relevant information,” he said.
KL Hockey ‘supported’ Gibbs through challenging period
In the email sent to parents on Wednesday, KL Hockey’s camp director Amanda Tayles wrote that Gibbs decided to step away from camp due to "recent attention" about a personal legal matter.
“KL Hockey is aware of Brad’s personal legal matter, which is unrelated to camp operations or his law enforcement duties, and has supported him through a difficult and challenging period in his personal life,” she wrote.
The email doesn't say that Gibbs was criminally charged, or that he pleaded guilty to those charges in April.
The same email includes a letter from Gibbs, where he writes that he’s taken full responsibility in court for a personal legal matter “and accepted accountability for my lapse in judgment.”
He said he made the decision to remove himself from all KL Hockey duties “out of respect for our players, families and the integrity of our summer camp.”
Gibbs wrote he was “deeply sorry to our community, our campers, our staff, our board, and the families who have placed their trust in me.”
“My focus right now is on continuing to take responsibility, learn from this experience, and rebuild that trust over time.”
KL Hockey’s Facebook account posted a video on Aug. 3, recapping its first week of activities, that shows Gibbs at a campsite. Two people who know Gibbs confirmed it was him.
Gibbs is also pictured on the camp’s “About Us” webpage. Several posts on his personal Facebook reference the camp, most recently from November 2024.
KL Hockey's day programming runs out of the Lindsay Recreation Complex, which is owned by the City of Kawartha Lakes. The city doesn’t require camps that use its facilities to request criminal record checks or vulnerable sector checks from their staff, the director of community services, Jenn Johnson, said in an email.
The camp’s overnight accommodations are located at Camp Endobanah, a non-profit camp available for rent that’s also in Kawartha Lakes. CBC News asked Camp Endobanah about its vetting process for camps that rent its facilities, but did not hear back before deadline.
Parents advised to ask about camp staff vetting
It’s unclear what vetting standards KL Hockey has for its staff, since it is not a member of the OCA. The provincial camp association has a publicly-available document of over 600 standards for its members, reviewed annually.
Those standards include a mandatory requirement that camps obtain a criminal record check from each staff member over 18 before employing them.
Camps have discretion over how they use information from criminal record checks, said Rankin Middlebrook, who is on the OCA board of directors and former chair of its standards review committee.
He said individual camps should determine appropriate steps based on the information in a check and the surrounding context.
The OCA also has an optional standard that camps request criminal record checks once every three years from returning staff members.
Middlebrook said he doesn’t think camps have to be OCA-accredited to be a “good camp,” but accredited camps must follow a higher standard. He said parents can review the OCA standards document so they can make an informed decision when picking a camp for their children.
Meanwhile, Tiwari said parents should do their due diligence by inquiring how summer camps are vetting their staff. But he added parents are entitled to expect a “safe system” and aren’t expected to become private investigators.
If a camp chooses to keep a staff member despite concerns, Tiwari said parents’ options are limited, due to the lack of legislation in this area.
“There's really nothing that can be done, other than parents demanding a refund or pulling their kids and speaking with their wallets,” he said.

Srinagar, Aug 18: The Economic Offences Wing (EOW) Kashmir of Crime Branch J&K has filed a chargesheet against a Budgam resident for allegedly attempting to influence a Crime Branch investigation after transferring ten thousand rupees to the bank account of one of the investigating officers as a bribe, officials said on Tuesday.
The officials said that the chargesheet was filed against Ghulam Ahmad Ganie, son of Ghulam Mohammad Ganie, a resident of Mirgund in Budgam district, before the Court of the Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Srinagar, in connection with FIR No. 28/2026, registered under Section 8 of the Prevention of Corruption Act and Sections 228 and 229 of the BNS.
In an official statement, a CBK spokesperson said the investigation was initiated on the basis of a written complaint alleging that the accused, who is also an accused in the ongoing investigation of FIR No. 11/2021 of Crime Branch Kashmir, now EOW Kashmir, transferred an amount of Rs. 10,000/- into the bank account of an Investigation Officer with the alleged intention of bribing and influencing the investigation in the said case
"Upon receipt of the complaint, a probe was ordered. During the course of investigation, the allegations were thoroughly examined and relevant evidence was collected. The investigation established the involvement of the accused in the alleged act, following which the chargesheet was prepared and presented before the Hon’ble Court for judicial determination in accordance with law," the statement said.
The general public has been advised not to offer or pay bribes to any public servant for obtaining any favour or service.
"Any demand for bribe or involvement in corrupt practices should be immediately reported to the competent authorities for necessary legal action," he said, adding that "Public cooperation and timely reporting are essential to curb corruption and promote transparency and accountability."

North Macedonian filmmaker Teona Mitevska (“Mother”) is prepping a sequel to her satirical drama “God Exists, Her Name is Petrunya,” which premiered in competition at the Berlinale in 2019, the director revealed at the Sarajevo Film Festival.
Written by Mitevska and Elma Tataragić, “Petra Doesn’t Want to Die (Anatomy of Masculinity)” is the story of a rebellious teenage feminist from Belgium who, despite being diagnosed with anorexia, bipolar disorder, OCD and trichotillomania, remains strong, determined and lucid in her conviction to do what she believes she must: leave this world.
That impulse takes her to North Macedonia, a country that seems to the Belgian teen to be stuck in time, if not at the ends of the Earth. There she meets Nenad, a millennial incel living in the provincial town of Makedonska Kamenica, who forges an unlikely pact with Petra, offering to help her take her own life.
Popular on Variety
Drawing a connection with the earlier dramedy “God Exists,” Mitevska described “Petra Doesn’t Want to Die” as “a continuation, a reinterpretation, or a counterpoint to” its predecessor, which won the Ecumenical Jury prize after its premiere in Berlin.
“God Exists” followed frustrated thirtysomething Petrunya (Zorica Nusheva), a determined yet endlessly put-upon woman still living with her parents in the dead-end Macedonian town of Štip. After throwing herself into an annual Orthodox ceremony traditionally reserved for men, she provoked a fiercely misogynistic backlash from the community. But Petrunya unapologetically stood her ground, setting her apart from — and at odds with — “a patriarchal Macedonia in the grips of bullying machismo and hidebound religion,” as Variety’s Jay Weissberg wrote in his review.
“Ten years after ‘God Exists, Her Name is Petrunya,’ here we are: Macedonia, 2026,” Mitevska told Variety in Sarajevo. “A single question stays imprinted in my head: Where are the Petrunyas of today?”
A sympathetic portrait of generation alpha, or what she dubbed “the anxious generation,” “Petra Doesn’t Want to Die” is “a response to and a testament to the power of new generations and their refusal to accept hypocrisy and involuntary/voluntary submission as the only remaining option.”
“In a world where young lives are like apples falling from trees, with alarming suicide rates rising daily,” said the director, “where future job prospects are not what they were, and the influence of the algorithm and social media paralyzes the agency of the individual and renders it to voluntary submission, the haunting question is: What is left for Petra [and her generation] to do?”
Mitevska said “Petra Doesn’t Want to Die” was inspired in part by a Q&A session during the promotional run of “God Exists,” when an audience member in a small German town asked, “Why are these men so angry?”
The question sparked a curiosity about the manosphere and its many offshoots and subcultures: the men’s rights movement, androphilia, paleo masculinity and other adherents of a “red pill philosophy” that “concentrates on restoring man’s natural capacity,” Mitevska said. That, in turn, led her to the character of Nenad, a proud Macedonian man and member of the Legion of Truth, a distinctly Balkan interpretation of the American MAGA movement.
“In his attempt to reassert himself, to affirm his masculinity, he is ready to do anything,” said the director. By contrast, Petra is a willful woman marked by “her strength and defiance.” The film explores what happens when those two worlds collide, telling the story of “two people who are complete opposites and who, in exceptional circumstances, in the very heart of chaos, find common ground,” Mitevska said, adding: “Through the study of masculinity, I also examine femininity, and vice versa.”
Mitevska is kicking off a busy week at the Sarajevo Film Festival. Unspooling in the festival’s main competition is “Skateboarding Is Not for Girls,” from North Macedonian debutante Dina Duma, which premiered at Tribeca and is produced by Sisters and Brother Mitevski, the production company co-founded by Teona and her siblings Labina and Vuk.
Meanwhile, in the CineLink industry section’s drama strand, Mitevska and Slovenian filmmaker Sonja Prosenc are pitching “Little Yugoslavia,” a dark comedy-horror series set in a post-socialist apartment complex where residents vanish without a trace, and two vampire queens are on a mission to purify the world.
As Variety exclusively revealed, Mitevska is also partnering with French filmmaker Céline Sciamma (“Portrait of a Lady on Fire”) and others at the Balkan fest to launch Sister Sister, an initiative that looks to reshape the role of women in the film and TV industries and create an inclusive and sustainable screen sector.
Mitevska’s last film, “Mother,” which starred Noomi Rapace as a young Mother Teresa, opened the Horizons strand of the Venice Film Festival last year.
The Sarajevo Film Festival runs Aug. 14 – 21.

13 ఆగస్టు 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన ఒక కార్యక్రమంలో ప్రధాని మోదీ విదేశాంగ విధానంపై విమర్శలు చేస్తూ, వేదికపై ఉన్న పార్టీ నేత సందీప్ దీక్షిత్ను రాహుల్ గాంధీ సరదాగా ఆలింగనం చేసుకున్నారు. ఆ సమయంలో, ఇటలీ ప్రధాని జార్జియా మెలోనిని ఉద్దేశిస్తూ వారు కొన్ని వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు. ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలను తీవ్రంగా ఖండిస్తూ, ఇటలీ ప్రధాని పట్ల ఇటువంటి వ్యాఖ్యలు చేయడం ఆమోదయోగ్యం కాదని భారతదేశంలోని ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయం ఒక అధికారిక ప్రకటన జారీ చేసినట్లు సోషల్ మీడియాలో ఒక ప్రకటన(ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఇటలీ ప్రధాని జార్జియా మెలోనిని ఉద్దేశించి రాహుల్ గాంధీ, సందీప్ దీక్షిత్ చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను ఖండిస్తూ భారత్లోని ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయం జారీ చేసిన ప్రకటన.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ ప్రకటనను భారత్లోని ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయం జారీ చేయలేదు. దీనిని ఒక సెటైర్ (వ్యంగ్య) X ఖాతా పోస్ట్ చేసింది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, భారతదేశంలోని ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయం ఇలాంటి ప్రకటన ఏదైనా జారీ చేసిందా అని తెలుసుకోవడానికి వారి అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్, సోషల్ మీడియా ఖాతాలను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరిశీలించగా, ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు లభించలేదు.
వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ ప్రకటన ‘italy in India’ పేరుతో ఉన్న ‘@AINga5f’ ఐడీ యొక్క X (ట్విట్టర్) ఖాతా నుండి మొదట పోస్ట్ అయినట్లు గుర్తించాం. అయితే, ఈ ఖాతా ఒక ‘సెటైర్’ (వ్యంగ్య) అకౌంట్ అని దాని బయోలో పేర్కొన్నారు. ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయానికి చెందిన అధికారిక X ఖాతాలో (@ItalyinIndia) మాత్రం ఎలాంటి ప్రకటన జారీ కాలేదు.
ఈ విషయంపై ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయాన్ని The Quint సంప్రదించగా, వైరల్ అవుతున్న ప్రకటన తమ కార్యాలయం నుంచి వెలువడలేదని, అది నకిలీదని వెల్లడించారు. ఈ అంశంపై అధికారిక వివరణ కోరుతూ మేము ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయాన్ని సంప్రదించాం. వారి నుంచి స్పందన రాగానే ఈ ఆర్టికల్ అప్డేట్ చేయబడుతుంది.
చివరిగా, ఇటలీ ప్రధాని జార్జియా మెలోనిపై రాహుల్ గాంధీ, సందీప్ దీక్షిత్ చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను ఇటలీ రాయబార కార్యాలయం ఖండించిందంటూ ప్రచారంలో ఉన్న ఈ ప్రకటన ఫేక్ది.

Apple Watches are smart little gadgets, but they don't always fit the vibe. There were plenty of nights when I left mine at home because, as much as I wanted to check my notifications discreetly, the watch just didn't match my outfit. I've also had my fair share of faux pas and just let the neon orange sport band clash with my neutral ensemble.
Fortunately, Apple Watch bands are a simple and relatively affordable way to zhuzh up the look of your wearable. Beyond aesthetics, different styles also impact performance and functionality. For example, I don't want a heavy stainless steel or high-quality leather band weighing me down during a sweaty workout, just as I wouldn't wear a flimsy silicone band to a dinner party.
At WIRED, we've been testing bands since the very first Apple Watch launched in 2015. After years of wearing and swapping, I've rounded up the best bands for every occasion. Be sure to check out our related product guides, including the Best Apple Watch Accessories, Best Apple Watch, and Best Smartwatches for more recommendations.
Featured in This Guide
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Updated August 2026: I added a comparison chart, along with the Apple Sport Band to Honorable Mentions. Prices and links were also updated.
How I Test Apple Watch Bands
I research Apple Watch bands across major retailers, including Apple, Amazon, and Nike. I also consulted former WIRED editor Adrienne So, who had covered fitness trackers and Apple Watch bands for a decade. I look for bestsellers, affordable dupes, and niche finds.
I test Apple Watch bands all day, every day, across workouts, commutes, and overnight. Each band is worn for at least two weeks and subjected to sweat, water, and everyday friction. That's typically enough time to evaluate comfort, quality, and durability. If it's severely uncomfortable or triggers skin irritation on the first day of testing, it is ruled out. My top picks remain in my rotation for months so I can compare them against newer models and assess how they hold up over time.
- Comfort: Apple Watch bands shouldn't pinch, trap moisture, or feel insecure. I also pay attention to breathability and potential irritation, especially with silicone and metal bands, and factor in how different skin types might react over time.
- Quality: Closures are fastened, unfastened, and adjusted repeatedly to see how they hold up. A good band should lock in place, adjust easily with one hand, and resist loosening over time. I also examine materials for flexibility, finish, and overall craftsmanship.
- Durability: To test claims of water resistance, I wear each band while I wash my hands, trek through the Chicago rain, and shower (if the brand says it's safe). Whenever relevant, I revisit bands after extended wear. I track discoloration, odor retention, and hardware fatigue.
- Ease of setup and use: I swap bands across multiple Apple Watch case sizes to ensure the lugs slide in easily and lock securely. I also judge how easy they are to install and remove.
- Adjustability and sizing: I test fit across a range of wrist sizes—with help from former WIRED editors Adrienne So and Martin Cizmar—and note whether the brands offer inclusive sizing.
- Versatility: I wear each band in casual, work, and dressier settings to see how well it adapts to different environments. I also note whether it complements different finishes and case colors.
Most of the Apple Watch bands remain in storage so I can continue long-term testing and compare newer releases against older models. Any discontinued models are donated once testing is complete.
What Am I Testing Next?
I'm testing the Nomad Sport Band. I'm also reevaluating the Nomad Tempo Band, the Apple Trail Loop, and the Apple Milanese Titanium Band.
Best Band for Everyday Wear
The Nike Sport Loop has been my everyday band since 2020. I bought another in 2023 because I wanted to swap colors, and I figured after three years, I should buy a brand-new one, but it has held up remarkably well. Made from a blend of recycled polyester, spandex, and nylon, it's breathable and lightweight. The double-layered nylon weave is designed with dense loops that help prevent moisture from getting trapped against your skin. As long as you regularly hand-wash it to rid it of sweat buildup and dirt, it stays odor-free.
The hook-and-loop fastener and pull tab make it easy to adjust with one hand. It is Velcro, so beware—it can snag on softer fabrics. Still, for a band designed with sports in mind, it's understated enough to wear almost anywhere. I wouldn't wear it to a formal event, but for the office or casual social events, it's perfect.

Best Titanium Apple Watch Band
Nomad originally designed the Stratos Band for the Apple Watch Ultra, but it fits just as well with the SE and Series 1 through 11. It's easy to adjust, refined enough for the office, and backed by Grade 4 titanium hardware with a scratch-resistant DLC coating. FKM rubber links (PFA-free and antimicrobial, according to Nomad) add flexibility, durability, and water resistance. The clasp is made with corrosion-resistant N52 magnets, which make it effortless to snap on, and it's designed with a manual release button, so you don't have to worry about it accidentally falling off. It's technically suited for workouts and outdoor use, but it is a hefty band that I personally prefer for casual everyday wear.
The hardware comes in natural or black finishes, which is nice if you're particular about matching your setup. The FKM rubber comes in four different colorways, including a limited-edition icy blue that glows in the dark. Demand for artificially generated smut is surging. But the quality of the visual content being created and shared—like on companion apps, where adult performers are selling their likeness to give fans a 24/7 experience, WIRED reported in March—isn’t exactly movie-level caliber.
Rogue Studio, a cinematic AI-generator platform built around adult visual storytelling, is trying to change that. Launching today, the studio, which bills itself as a “playground for creative ethical mischief,” plans to deliver industry-level video production without creative and sexual restrictions. Its marquee product is Rogue 1.0, an AI video-generation tool for making uncensored adult content that is comparable to other pro-level models Hollywood is using.
“There really isn’t a place for a sophisticated creator to go make content that’s rated R. Either they go to these skeezy NSFW sites that are built on outdated open-source tech, or they try to do high-quality stuff but they’re censored up the gills,” a Rogue Studio cofounder, who goes by Mr. Rogue, tells WIRED. “It’s a very fine line between being a sophisticated platform for adults versus becoming just a porn site. And we do not want the latter. We want to do what HBO did for television.”
Rogue, which has subscription tiers ranging from $29 to $299, offers all the safe-for-work frontier models within its system—similar to Higgsfield, it includes NanoBanana, Seedance, Kling 2.0, and others—in addition to its own proprietary models for generating adult-oriented images and video. Using the platform, you can employ multiple elements from several different AI-generator models when drumming up ideas.
Let’s say you have a concept for a freaky sci-fi horror short. You could potentially start ideating on a zombie character using Midjourney, then use Rogue’s AI tools to add more high-definition uncensored features to the character.
According to its terms of service, Rogue prohibits user-generated images or videos for training, and it strictly forbids the creation or distribution of nonconsensual deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, unauthorized depictions of public figures, and other illegal or abusive imagery.
In an effort to prevent bad actors from using the platform to make these prohibited visuals, Rogue has three layers of human moderation. The first is at the prompt level, which searches for keywords and flags them for possible account suspension if it is determined that there is clear illegal intent. The next layer is inside the system, called the intention layer. Bad actors might try to outsmart moderators by slightly misspelling a real actor’s name to generate a deepfake image, so moderators will reread the prompt to assess the user’s intent. The final layer analyzes the image or video created before it is shared with the user. For example, if a user prompts “famous blonde singer” and the image generated looks like Taylor Swift, the image won’t get delivered.
Mr. Rogue tells WIRED that he and his fellow cofounder, both of whom are movie producers, have decided not to disclose their names because of the “real risk” involved in being associated with creating erotic-themed work. “Because of the climate right now in Hollywood and working in AI, you have got to be very careful,” Mr. Rogue says. (WIRED verified that the pair of founders do, in fact, work in Hollywood; they have produced movies with a combined box office of over $2 billion.)
In the wake of the 2023 Hollywood strikes, where labor unions fought to secure guardrails against the unapproved digital likenesses of actors appearing in films and TV, leading studios have been assessing ways to incorporate AI into productions with the goal of lowering expenses.
The friction has led to AI being seen as unfavorable and has created a stigma around it. Rogue’s cofounders know this but don’t want to shy away from the tech’s creative potential.
The reality is that AI is no longer a distant possibility for Hollywood. Computers are already working behind the scenes to animate preproduction storyboards and create a more efficient editing process, such as polishing VFX effects and audio. Netflix recently revealed that 300 of its shows use generative AI. The integration is happening at a scale bigger than many viewers realize, Matt Belloni, a founding partner at Puck who covers the business of Hollywood, told WIRED earlier this month.
Since 2000, sex scenes in movies have declined by 40 percent, according to a 2023 study conducted by The Economist. But recent releases suggest that the industry may be turning a corner. “Movies are getting horny again,” one film critic who specializes in erotic thrillers told the BBC. According to a recent survey from entertainment research firm Luminate, despite an overall backlash against AI in Hollywood, one-third of consumers now feel indifferent toward the use of AI in production across all areas, except when it comes to writing and acting.
Rogue is making a bet that the continued adoption of AI tools—particularly ones focused on delivering premium visuals—could potentially supercharge that experience for viewers to the point where the quality of a performer’s delivery isn’t determined by whether it is AI or not, the cofounder says.
“We’re so used to uncensored meaning you get a fraction of the quality. Right now too much of the art form is being lost.”

A PhD scholar at Delhi University's Faculty of Law has been suspended after CCTV footage allegedly showed him slapping a professor on campus, with the incident prompting the university to order an inquiry. The accused has been identified as Shubham Singh, who was admitted to the Faculty of Law during the 2024-25 academic session. According to a report by India Today, CCTV footage shows Singh waiting near the entrance of a campus building before walking towards Law Faculty professor Umang Bhawan and allegedly slapping him. Other students who were present at the location can be seen attempting to intervene after the alleged assault. Delhi University has taken immediate action against Singh following the incident. University Proctor Manoj Kumar Singh confirmed that the incident took place on Monday morning and said a committee had been formed to investigate the matter, according to the report. The Proctor's Office, in its suspension order, said Singh was suspended from the Faculty of Law with immediate effect. The university has also barred him from entering any Delhi University premises while the inquiry is pending. An independent three-member inquiry committee comprising professors has been constituted to examine the incident and establish the circumstances surrounding the confrontation. The panel is expected to look into what led to the incident and determine what further action should be taken. The incident has drawn condemnation from sections of the teaching community. The Democratic Teachers' Front (DTF) described the episode as the third recent case involving violence or physical aggression against teachers, India Today reported, citing the teachers' organisation. The DTF has criticised the university administration's handling of campus violence, alleging that its response has been slow and insufficient. The teachers' body has argued that suspension alone may not be enough to prevent similar incidents and has called for stronger action to protect faculty members. According to the report, the DTF also claimed that professors had previously faced verbal abuse from another Faculty of Law student. The organisation has demanded measures to ensure the safety and dignity of teachers on campus. The latest incident has also brought attention to a similar confrontation reported at Dr Bhim Rao Ambedkar College, a Delhi University-affiliated institution, in October 2025. DU Students' Union Joint Secretary Deepika Jha was accused of slapping professor Sujit Kumar during a disciplinary committee meeting. The incident was captured on video and led to protests, with teachers calling for action from the university. Delhi University later suspended Jha for two months and barred her from entering DU-affiliated colleges in her capacity as a student leader. The action was criticised by some members of the teaching community, who considered it inadequate, according to the report. The DTF has cited the earlier episode while questioning whether the university has been sufficiently firm in dealing with alleged violence against teachers. The three-member committee will now examine the latest incident involving Singh and professor Umang Bhawan. The inquiry is expected to establish the circumstances that led to Monday's confrontation and recommend further action based on its findings. Until then, Singh remains suspended from the Faculty of Law and barred from entering Delhi University premises. The incident has once again put the spotlight on concerns raised by teachers over alleged aggression on university campuses and calls for stronger institutional mechanisms to address such cases. A video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi moving around a stage greeting people while the national anthem plays in the background is viral on social media, with users claiming that the Prime Minister was being disrespectful to the anthem.
An user on Facebook, Kumar Raj, shared the purported video on August 15, Independance Day, with Modi circled out. The post has garnered 2.3 million views. It was shared around 14,000 times and has received 30,500 reactions.
Activist Piyush Manush shared the same video on Facebook, which was viewed over 76,000 times.
Several X users also amplified the viral video, amplifying the same claim.
Fact Check
A keyframe in the viral video showed a screen placed on the podium which mentioned the location of the event as Jasauli Kharag, located in Bihar’s Siwan city. The date mentioned was June 20, 2025.
A relevant keyword search led us to the original video uploaded from the Prime Minister’s official YouTube channel. In this video dated June 21, 2025, Modi, seen in the same attire as the viral video, walked onto a stage while he was being introduced by the speaker. Amid cheers from the audience, he waved to them and shook hands with other dignitaries present on the stage. At no point can the national anthem be heard playing in the clip.
Thus, the claim that Prime Minister Narendra Modi disrespected the national anthem by walking around the stage while it played is misleading. The original video shows Modi being introduced by the speaker and waving to a cheering audience, with no national anthem playing in the clip. The anthem heard in the viral version was added later to the original video, altering the context of the footage to amplify a false claim.

Dutch officials have warned that a high-severity macOS vulnerability that allows attackers to execute malicious code is under active exploitation.
“The NCSC has received a notification indicating that active abuse of this vulnerability has been observed on multiple systems on which port 5900 was accessible from the Internet,” the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centrum warned earlier this week. “In all these cases, root had been accessed on the affected system and a Monero crypto miner had been placed.”
Do you know if your screen sharing is on?
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-65400, received a patch from Apple last week for macOS Tahoe, Sequoia, and Sonoma. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 7.1 out of 10, stems from a bug in the macOS screen sharing capability, which allows a remote party to view the screen and control the keyboard and mouse while a machine is turned on. A flaw in the “state management,” which keeps track of preceding events, user interactions, variables, and other system states, is the underlying cause.
A video of the exploit in action can be found here. Details of CVE-2026-65400 became public at last week’s Black Hat security conference. Apple said last week that CVE-2026-65400 “may” allow an attacker without credentials to gain access to a Mac. It’s unclear why Apple hedged, but softening language is common among most tech developers when disclosing vulnerabilities.

Lower yuan borrowing costs and longer maturities lure issuers, marking a fresh phase in the city’s expanding offshore market
2-MIN READ2-MIN
Hong Kong’s offshore yuan bond market has seen another record-breaking deal – the largest single issuance by a Chinese state-owned enterprise – underscoring the growing appeal of the city’s dim sum bond market.
State Grid Corporation of China raised 14.9 billion yuan (US$2.2 billion) through offshore yuan-denominated bonds, known as dim sum bonds, according to a statement on Monday from Bank of China, which acted as a joint global coordinator for the deal.
The offering comprised 3.9 billion yuan of five-year bonds priced to yield 1.86 per cent, 7 billion yuan of 10-year notes at 2.18 per cent and 4 billion yuan of 20-year debt at 2.46 per cent.
Investor demand reached a record high, with orders totalling 193.8 billion yuan, more than 13 times the amount on offer, according to the bank.
The deal comes as Hong Kong’s dim sum bond market continues to expand. Nearly 500 billion yuan of offshore yuan bonds were sold in the first seven months of the year, according to Bank of China. The lender said it underwrote more than 100 billion yuan during the period.
Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, speaking at an August 3 event, said annual dim sum bond issuance had reached 1 trillion yuan in the past two years, with the outstanding bond size standing at around 1.6 trillion yuan.

- According to reposts of the rumor, Hall attempted to share 2 Chronicles 7:14, an Old Testament Bible verse some people have quoted to support their belief the that Founding Fathers established the U.S. as a Christian nation.

In July and August 2026, Facebook users reposted a years-old rumor about religion and technology. The posts featured copied-and-pasted text alleging Facebook removed a Bible verse post a user named Jennifer Wilson Hall shared.
For example, one post (archived) from July 25 read as follows:
Earlier today, Jennifer Wilson Hall had a post removed by Facebook stating the content "did not meet their community standards". Well, below is the bible verse that was removed. I am asking that everyone who sees this, please post the verse also.
2 Chronicles 7:14,
"If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land. "🙏
God bless America! I am asking that everyone who sees this to please post the verse also.
I copied & pasted. Won't you?
A silent nation is a defeated nation!
God is on High!! He's still in control! His Son Jesus Christ IS the only way!! Amen!!@
The posts displayed 2 Chronicles 7:14, an Old Testament Bible verse some people have quoted to support their belief the that Founding Fathers established the U.S. as a Christian nation.
A Snopes reader previously asked (archived) about this matter in the Snopes Tips Facebook group. We also received numerous reader emails and website searches over the years from people wanting to find out if Facebook truly removed a Bible verse a woman named Jennifer Wilson Hall posted.
Snopes has not yet located enough evidence to definitively confirm or debunk this rumor. As such, we have not yet established a fact-check rating for this article. We will add updates should we uncover further details.
To learn more, we contacted Meta and a Facebook user matching Hall's name. That specific person named Jennifer Wilson Hall told us by phone she knew nothing about the matter. We also reached out to an apparent friend of Hall's named Ron Swindall who appeared to originate the copied-and-pasted posts with a post tagging Hall's profile. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Researching the rumor
Searches for the copied-and-pasted text claiming Facebook removed Hall's Bible verse post found posts as far back as May 2020, prior to the creation of the Meta parent company name in 2021. The searches located other 2020 posts, as well.
According to those searches, a Facebook user named Ron Swindall created the oldest public-facing post (archived) on May 16, 2020. His post featured a tagged link for a woman's profile matching Hall's name living in Mississippi — the same Hall who told us by phone she had no knowledge of Facebook removing a Bible verse post.
(Ron Swindall accessed via Facebook)
In Swindall's post, he called Hall a "good friend." His post's inclusion of the words "copied and pasted" appeared to only pertain to the second part of the text with the Bible verse. Swindall previously tagged Hall in other posts, including another one in which he called her a friend.
Users commenting under Swindall's post alleged Facebook had also removed their posts containing Bible verses or statements about Christianity. They did not include evidence with their comments.
One commenter under Swindall's post asked if the alleged original Hall post Facebook supposedly took down featured text other than the Bible verse that possibly factored into its removal. For example, searches found many people and pages sharing the same verse in 2020 along with large chunks of text about a wide variety of subjects.
Commenters under reposts containing the Hall story and Bible verse accurately noted Meta had not removed those posts, reassuring some users that the company had not sought to permanently and widely censor or remove Christian content — a rumor we've reported on in the past.
Meta's website says the company "uses technology and review teams to detect, review and take action on millions of pieces of content every day on Facebook and Instagram." As of the 2020s, that technology included the presence of Meta's own artificial intelligence. The company's documentation acknowledges the automated moderation system can make mistakes, saying "we still have work to do" and that they want to "make sure review teams spend more time focused on the right decisions."

Stomach pain is one of the most common symptoms people experience. It can range from mild discomfort caused by indigestion or gas, to severe pain caused by conditions such as appendicitis, gallstones, pancreatitis or intestinal obstruction.
Doctors say the site, severity, onset, duration and progression of the pain, along with other symptoms, can provide important clues about its cause. However, the intensity of pain alone does not always indicate how serious the underlying problem is.
“Some people with a serious condition may have only mild discomfort, while others with a less serious problem may experience severe pain,” says S. Jennie, professor, department of general Medicine, SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, Chennai.
Where it hurts
The location of abdominal pain can sometimes point to the organ involved. Burning or discomfort in the upper abdomen or lower chest may occur with acid-peptic disorders. Pain in the right upper abdomen, particularly after meals, can occur with gallbladder disease. Severe upper abdominal pain that radiates to the back may be seen in pancreatitis.
Pain that begins around the navel and later moves to the lower right side may occur with appendicitis. Pain in the lower abdomen or side may also occur with kidney stones.
However, these patterns are only clues and should not be used for self-diagnosis, says Arul Prakash, gastroenterologist, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai. “It is difficult to differentiate between a minor and major problem based only on pain,” he says.
Mild, short-lived pain that improves after passing stools or gas, resting or drinking fluids is generally less concerning. In contrast, sudden, severe, localised, persistent or progressively worsening pain should be assessed by a doctor.
Watch for warning signs
The symptoms accompanying abdominal pain often provide a better indication of urgency than the pain alone. Persistent vomiting can cause dehydration and may also occur with intestinal obstruction. Fever may suggest infection or inflammation.
Blood in vomit or stools should never be ignored. Black, tar-like stools or coffee-ground-like vomit can indicate bleeding in the digestive tract. Severe diarrhoea, particularly with high fever, severe pain or blood in stools, also requires medical assessment.
Increasing abdominal swelling, especially when accompanied by vomiting or an inability to pass stools or gas, can indicate bowel obstruction. Yellowing of the eyes or skin may point to a problem involving the liver, gallbladder or bile ducts.
The SHARP warning signs
Dr. Jennie suggests remembering the SHARP warning signs: sudden or severe pain; associated symptoms such as vomiting, fever, bleeding, jaundice or confusion; advanced age, particularly with chronic illnesses; rigidity or marked tenderness of the abdomen; and pain during pregnancy or after surgery.
Chest pain or difficulty breathing along with upper abdominal pain also warrants urgent assessment, as some heart conditions can mimic abdominal discomfort. Dr. Arul Prakash notes that patients have occasionally mistaken heart attack symptoms for acidity and treated themselves with over-the-counter medicines.
Avoid self-treatment
A common mistake is to assume that every episode of abdominal pain is due to ‘gas’ or acidity. Repeatedly taking medicines without establishing the cause can delay diagnosis.
Painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin can irritate the stomach and increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding in susceptible people. They should not be taken casually for unexplained abdominal pain.
An antacid may provide temporary relief for occasional, familiar acidity or heartburn. But symptoms that persist for several days, keep returning or become progressively worse need medical evaluation. Antibiotics should also not be started without medical advice, particularly for diarrhoea, as many common gastrointestinal infections are viral and do not require them.
Children, older adults and pregnant women need particular caution. Children may have difficulty describing their symptoms, while older adults can have serious abdominal conditions with relatively mild or atypical pain. During pregnancy, abdominal pain may have benign causes but can also indicate pregnancy-related or surgical emergencies.
People with previous abdominal surgery, gallstones, inflammatory bowel disease or chronic liver, kidney or other major illnesses should also seek medical advice sooner when they develop new or unusual pain.
Doctors say, is not to judge abdominal pain only by how much it hurts. A new, persistent or worsening pain, particularly when accompanied by warning signs, should not be dismissed as acidity or gas.

Hong Kong court orders defunct Apple Daily to pay HK$1.5 million over defamatory articles
Judge says Apple Daily failed to prove its allegations or allow China Innovation Investment and its executives to respond before publication
A Hong Kong court has ordered the defunct Apple Daily newspaper to pay HK$1.5 million in damages to a listed company and two senior executives over 10 defamatory articles that accused them of spying on the city’s pro-democracy activists at Beijing’s behest.
Mr Justice Tony Poon Siu-tung found that the articles exposed China Innovation Investment, its chairman Xiang Xin and his wife, alternate director Kung Ching, to contempt and ridicule.
Poon said the newspaper had failed to prove that the allegations were true or to give the company and its executives an opportunity to respond before the reports were published between November 23 and December 7, 2019.
He ordered Apple Daily Limited and AD Internet Limited, which were the newspaper’s publisher and Internet domain name owner, respectively, to pay HK$400,000 to HK$600,000 in damages to the three plaintiffs, totalling HK$1.5 million.
The articles followed allegations made in November 2019 by self-proclaimed former spy William Wang Liqiang, who claimed that the Communist Party of China had used China Innovation as a front to interfere in Hong Kong politics by infiltrating political groups, universities and media outlets.

China censors public mourning as it holds former premier's funeral
- Published
Flags at government sites are flying at half-mast and security vehicles are parked in the heart of Beijing, as China mourns former Premier Zhu Rongji.
Zhu died of an illness last week at 97, and will be cremated at a funeral in Beijing on Tuesday. There has not been footage from the ceremony, which is being kept low-key.
Zhu, who served as China's premier from 1998 to 2003, is remembered as one of the country's most important economic reformers.
While hailing the late premier as a "loyal" party member, the Chinese state is also wary that public mourning for his era of reform can easily turn into veiled criticisms of the current government, under Xi Jinping.
After his death, state media has described Zhu as an "outstanding member of the Chinese Communist Party" and "time-tested and loyal Communist fighter".
But on the internet, posts about Zhu have been contained and censored - like an essay written by economist Zhao Jian, which remembered Zhu's era as a time when people were "properly poor" but saw a clear future ahead.
"There were no smartphones then, no short-form videos and no screens filled by the purveyors of anxiety," he wrote.
"The sky was blue, life moved slowly and people could say what they really thought."
His comments were removed from WeChat the day after publication.
The party has long been fearful of public reaction to deaths of senior officials and public figures.
The deaths of former premier Zhou Enlai in 1976 and Hu Yaobang, a former CCP general secretary, in 1989, prompted widespread outpourings of grief that morphed into protests.
Zhu died just days before the Communist Party leadership gathered to commemorate the birth centenary of President Jiang Zemin, who died in 2022.
The death of Zhu and Jiang, two such prominent leaders from the same era, has prompted a wave of nostalgia among many Chinese people for a time when the country looked as if it was going in a different direction - when it appeared that it may open to the world and allow more freedom for its people.
Candour of a bygone era
Previously purged under Mao Zedong's regime, Zhu was brought back into the fold after Mao's death in 1976.
Zhu served as premier alongside Jiang Zemin, who became Communist Party chief in 1989 and president in 1993.
The two men served alongside each other at the top of China's leadership from 1998 to 2003, leading China through an era of rapid economic growth and entry into global trade.
During that time, China pushed through painful changes: shuttering chronically unprofitable state firms, dismantling the old housing system in favour of a commercial property market, weathering the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s and joining the World Trade Organization in 2001.
But what appears to captivate Chinese people from that era was that both had a certain style - a common touch.
A Chinese state media documentary about Jiang Zemin's life shows him banging on tables one minute and erupting in laughter the next.
Zhu, meanwhile, once labelled rogue bankers as "half-wits" and described the flood dykes lining the Yangtze River as "flimsy and porous as tofu dregs".
He was also known for his deadpan humour, like at a news conference in 1999, when he was asked about allegations that China had donated to US President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party.
"If the political contribution were to be really that effective, and I have $146 billion of foreign exchange reserve, I can put out at least $10 billion for that purpose. Why just $300,000? That would be too foolish," he said, drawing laughter from the crowd.
The day he died, the Jiang Zemin documentary featured Zhu explaining how he persuaded his comrades to implement tough reforms.
"I'm not here to talk about pros and cons. I am here to talk about how to get things done," he is heard saying.
Circulating on social media is a picture of Jiang laughing together with Zhu and praised their candid communication.
"They told the truth, shouldered the responsibility and spared no effort in serving the people," the post read.
It's a style that has captivated Chinese audiences and stands in contrast with the current carefully choreographed leadership style.
Xi's narrative
The passing of the two leaders into China's history books marks a definitive end to the breakneck reforms of the 1990s and early 2000s, with an emphasis on private entrepreneurship and wealth creation.
That stands in contrast to President Xi, who has exerted greater central control and pressed a state-driven economic policy focused on technological autonomy and strategic industries.
In a 40-minute speech on Monday, Xi called on the Communist Party to carry forward Jiang's legacy, presenting the current leadership as the continuation of his political and ideological project.
"On the new journey ahead, we must heighten our sense of vigilance against potential dangers," he said during Monday's event.
"With an indomitable fighting spirit and superb skill in struggle," we must "proactively meet the major tests posed by high winds and rushing waters, or even by raging storms," he added.
He also praised Jiang's crackdown on a reformist Shanghai newspaper in 1989 after it voiced support for the pro-democracy demonstrations that culminated in the bloody Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
"Xi is committed to the great renaissance of the Chinese nation," says Kerry Brown, Professor of Chinese Studies and Director of the Law China Institute at King's College London.
"He's trying to put forward a unified historic narrative - any idea that their leadership offered or suggested a different future path will not be allowed a public airing," he adds.
"Instead, their lives will be knitted into the narrative that everything they did transformed China into what it is now, rather than dwell on any other 'What If's'."
But Xi now faces considerable challenges as China is facing slower economic growth and demographic decline.
House prices have plummeted, youth unemployment is high and factory output is becoming more sluggish.
The days of double-digit economic growth have gone.
This mourning for a bygone era is a mourning for a time when Chinese families felt that if they worked hard, their lives would improve.
For many, that certainty has gone.
As Zhao Jian wrote in his essay: "life was hard, but it was hardship sustained by hope."
He admits now many in China have "material abundance" and "skylines bristling with high-rises and streets teeming with traffic."
But why then, he asks, "do we feel so empty inside?"

A common cause given for leg pain is muscle strain, and this may be attributed to standing for a long time, exercising incorrectly, or getting older. But sometimes, there may be something different going on. A pain that begins in the lower back and radiates down the buttock and to the leg, may indicate irritation or pressure on the sciatic nerve, and is referred to as sciatica.
The largest nerve in the body is the sciatic nerve. It extends from the lower back through buttocks and down each leg. If a nerve in the lower back is compressed or inflamed, it may result in pain that radiates down this nerve.
How do you know if you have sciatica pain?
Sciatica isn’t always typical leg pain. It can cause a sudden electric-like, burning or tearing sensation down the back of the thigh and sometimes into the calf or foot from the lower back or buttock.
Some people may also experience tingling, numbness or weakness in the affected leg. The pain can worsen after sitting for prolonged periods, or after coughing, sneezing or certain movements.
In some cases, the discomfort may be primarily experienced in the leg, and there may be very little discomfort in the back. This can be one explanation as to why people may confuse sciatica with leg muscle or joint pain.
What causes sciatica?
A common cause of sciatica is a slipped disc or a bulging disc in the lower portion of the spine. The discs between the bones of our spine work like cushions. If one of them bulges or tears, it can compress an adjacent nerve.
Other reasons include changes in the spine with age, constriction of the spinal canal, bone growth and, less frequently, injury or other spinal diseases.
Not all people suffering from sciatica require a surgery. With the right kind of rest, and the use of the remedies as prescribed by a physician, physiotherapy and a gradual return to normal activity, many people get better. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the symptoms.
When to det a doctor’s advice
Some back or leg pain may get better over time, but certain symptoms shouldn’t be ignored. You should seek medical advice if the pain is severe, keeps returning, lasts for several weeks or is affecting your ability to walk, work or perform everyday activities.
Numbness or worsening weakness in the leg, trouble with urination or defecation or numbness around the inner thighs and genitals are emergencies.
Avoiding making every leg ache a diagnosis of sciatica is also important. Similar symptoms can occur due to problems involving the muscles, joints, blood vessels or other nerves, which is why it is important to consult a doctor. Your doctor can evaluate your symptoms, motion, muscle strength and reflexes and might suggest imaging if needed.
In addition to this, keeping a healthy weight, being physically active, strengthening core muscles and avoiding long periods of sitting can help keep your spine healthy.
The bottom line is: leg pain that radiates from the back or buttock is not necessarily from the leg and can be from the spine. Early identification of warning signs and proper diagnosis can prevent symptoms from becoming severe and can help to expedite a return to normal life.
(Dr. Kalidutta Das is chief and director of spine services, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. Kaliduttadas@gmail.com)

A main theme of the nine-book sci-fi series The Expanse is that sometimes you may never know the consequences of a choice you made. The universe, utterly indifferent black box that it is, “never tells us if we did right or wrong,” as the character Naomi Nagata puts it in The Expanse TV show.
That’s the line the developer of the upcoming Expanse video game has adopted as its own slogan. The Expanse: Osiris Reborn is set to release in spring 2027. It’s being developed by Owlcat Games, the Cyprus-based developer known for dense role-playing games like Pathfinder: Kingmaker and Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader.
Osiris Reborn is a third-person shooter and role-playing game where the player slips into the boots of a spaceship captain leading a found-family crew of misfits across the far-future solar system. You fight bad guys and float around in zero-gravity environments in the hard-science setting of The Expanse books and show. Dialog options and choice trees baked into cutscenes let you shape the narrative and change the outcomes. As many people have pointed out, it sounds very much like the Mass Effect video game series.
This will be the studio’s first third-person shooter, a departure for a company known for its top-down role-playing games. Owlcat Games beefed up its staff to build Osiris Reborn, and has faced criticism after releasing a beta version of the game in April. Players lauded the combat and visuals, but many found the story and voice acting lacking. (Apparently the game does not yet incorporate “Belter creole,” a language construct used by characters in The Expanse that has become a beloved part of the series.) It’s important to note that this was indeed a beta test, and the company has said it is aiming to fix some issues players have called attention to, even recasting a voice actor.
The Expanse is a complicated property to adapt, given that Osiris Reborn takes place around the same time as the first and second books of a nine-book series. Owlcat shared some details with WIRED about how it plans to implement choices in the story—moments where the player is faced with the opportunity to make a decision that affects the world and story that plays out.
You can choose a backstory and appearance for your character, but there are no skill classes. Your character is meant to develop based on the decisions you make. There are also choices for how you interact with your spaceship’s crew, and the ability to mentor them to advance their skills in different areas.
There are three competing factions (Earth, Mars, and the outer-space dwellers in the asteroid belt called Belters) you can work with and try to befriend. Owlcat Games says, “Keeping good relations with everyone won’t be easy—you’ll only get one chance to stay on everyone’s good side.”
It all sounds very much like decision-tier systems in games like Mass Effect. Will it compare to the truly transformative choices you can make in a game like Baldur’s Gate 3? Maybe not. Owlcat declined to speak with WIRED directly, but Leonid Rastorguev, the game's design director, replied to questions via email.
“This isn't our first game where the sheer number of choices and consequences is a core part of the experience,” Rastorguev wrote.
For Osiris Reborn, Owlcat is using an internal development system it calls Etudes to build a system of flags and triggers in the narrative that can help track player decisions, even small ones, and carry them forward in the game. Rastorguev says those choices can range from cosmetic changes, to ones that block off or unlock additional content, lead to a character dying, or change the ending.
According to critics who have reviewed the beta, the outcome of the choices isn’t immediately noticeable. One choice—where you have to pick between fighting and standing down from a battle—plays out nearly the same way in the moment no matter which option the player chooses. Owlcat says what beta players haven’t seen yet is “how far that decision ripples.”
“[Players] want to feel that they've left a mark on the universe itself,” Rastorguev wrote. “But The Expanse also has an established canon and major characters whose stories have already been told in the books and the TV series. It would feel strange for us to rewrite their fates, especially by introducing branching outcomes into events that are already firmly established.”
Rastorguev says the key to a successful choice system is to give players enough information to know that they’ve set something in motion, without necessarily giving them the entire chain of consequences. The events may be referenced again in conversations, in-game news reports, or changes in the world, and “can suggest that the consequences of your decision will continue long after you've moved on.”
If that holds, it will be very neat. For a game so influenced by Mass Effect, I do worry that Osiris Reborn might inadvertently recreate Mass Effect 3’s worst mistake, botching the ending of its series by limiting all the choices people had made across the games into three basic options to wrap everything up. Choice systems in games are great, but they often boil down into two or three big options at the end. (The game will have multiple endings, but Owlcat is not ready to say how many there will be or how different they are from one another.)
“We've put a lot of thought into this,” Rastorguev wrote, “and found ways for some of the player's choices to feel meaningful on the scale of the wider universe and potentially shape consequences that extend years beyond the immediate events of our story.”
Sounds like a real moonshot.
