Ambassador Bridge 'aggressively' pursued trucking clients amid Gordie Howe delay: industry rep
Union official representing some U.S. truck drivers described deal for lower tolls at Ambassador
As uncertainty swelled in recent months around the long-awaited opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, representatives from the privately-owned Ambassador Bridge up the Detroit River were “aggressively” pursuing trucking companies in an apparent bid to retain their business, according to an industry representative.
Lak Shoan, director of policy for the Ontario Trucking Association, said his organization started hearing from a “handful of members” about the bridge’s efforts around springtime.
“It wasn't something that they came to us with or anything like that,” he said. “It would just come up in conversations sort of, you know, ‘Have you heard that the Ambassador Bridge has been, you know, reaching out to more companies?’ And that's when we started hearing from a few more folks that this was occurring.”
CBC Windsor contacted several Canadian trucking companies with cross-border operations to ask if the Ambassador Bridge had approached them with toll rate offers. Those who answered said they couldn’t discuss private business agreements, while others simply did not respond.
But in a now-deleted post from late July, a U.S. trucking union official ordered his members not to use the new publicly-owned crossing because of a contract with the Ambassador Bridge in which they were saving $240,000 on tolls per month.
“If we wanted to begin using the Gordie Howe bridge, the Ambassador Bridge would first have to be notified that we intend to terminate the current contract,” wrote UAW Local 212 Chair JT Barrett, who represents FCA Transport (Stellantis) drivers.
- Gordie Howe bridge will cut deep into truck traffic at competing Ambassador Bridge: DHS
- The Ambassador Bridge has lost its spot as the busiest U.S.-Canada trade corridor
Toll rates and revenue were a key part of the months-long political saga to open the $6.4 billion Gordie Howe bridge, which the Canadian government paid for in full. The deal to open the crossing contains a provision giving the U.S. government the ability to block the new bridge from lowering tolls “below the average of comparable regional crossings.”
The wealthy Moroun family of Michigan, which has owned the Ambassador Bridge since 1979, ramped up its political influence efforts in the months before U.S. President Donald Trump suddenly threatened to block the new crossing from opening.
Though the bridge eventually opened to traffic on July 27, it came after a June opening was scrapped at the request of the U.S. government, according to Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Trump has been accused of trying to block the new bridge’s opening to benefit the Morouns.
Representatives for the Ambassador Bridge did not respond to questions before publication time. But a notice on their website suggests there is a cheaper toll program available to some trucking companies.
“Commercial customers with over 150 expected monthly crossings are eligible for new A-Pass Subscription Accounts,” the page reads. “These feature fixed monthly rates, determined based on expected crossings.”
- New bridge, same traffic: Why is the road to the Ambassador Bridge still packed with trucks?
- Michigan Senate candidate accuses Trump of keeping Canada-U.S. bridge closed to help donor
Shoan said the trucking association doesn’t know the exact details of what the bridge was offering companies, but he believes “it was around retention or trying to attract fleets to use the Ambassador Bridge.”
He said his group welcomes “healthy competition” between the bridges, which can lead to lower toll costs for trucking companies.
Barrett’s Facebook post provided some financial specifics about the deal he said FCA Transport has with the Ambassador Bridge.
“Under that contract, we pay a flat rate of $160,000 per month, regardless of how many crossings are made,” he said.
“Before this contract, we were paying north of $400,000 per month on a per-crossing basis,” he continued.
Barrett did not respond to a request for comment. Stellantis declined to confirm whether its FCA Transport drivers are under an exclusive toll contract with the Ambassador Bridge.
“The opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge strengthens the single most important border crossing in North America,” the global automaker said in a statement. “We are looking forward to using this additional crossing to support our just-in-time operations across our manufacturing operations in both countries, improving the flow of goods for an integrated industry that depends on seamless logistics. As a matter of company policy, Stellantis does not comment on proprietary information."
Shoan said the uncertainty around the Gordie Howe bridge’s opening would have made any deals offered by the Ambassador Bridge appealing to trucking firms.
“If you look at the current economic climate, which has been unsettled over the last several months, businesses are looking for certainty wherever you can find it,” he said. “If there's an opportunity to look for certainty from a cost perspective, [...] most business owners would definitely take that peace of mind.”

A rumor spread online in August 2026 that Massachusetts Democrats had installed a demonic statue in front of the state Capitol building. According to the claim, the statue was of Molech (also spelled Moloch, which is how we'll refer to the figure from here on), an ancient god who, according to multiple passages in the Old Testament, was related to child sacrifice.
(X user @Howodd69)
The story spread after Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat, signed a bill into law that makes it possible for all women to receive an abortion after 24 weeks of pregnancy, based on a physician's "professional medical judgment." (Anti-abortion advocates online suggested the state had legalized "abortion until birth," a claim Snopes separately fact-checked.)
Readers wrote in looking for more information on the supposed statue.
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If the statue were real, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or The Boston Globe, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We didn't find any credible reporting about the Moloch statue. The story originated with The Babylon Bee, a satirical news site that describes itself as a "Trusted Source for Christian News Satire." The Babylon Bee originally posted the story on Aug. 13, 2026.
Snopes has alerted readers to several instances of rumors originating from satirical articles published by The Babylon Bee, including a fictitious story suggesting that new government-run grocery stores in New York City would require shoppers to have a "special mark" on their hand or forehead — the number 666, often associated with Satan or the Antichrist.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Google is reportedly planning to move all Pixel production out of China
The company will most likely manufacture its Pixel devices in Vietnam and India starting in 2027, Nikkei Asia says.
Google will no longer manufacture any Pixel device in China starting next year, according to Nikkei Asia. The company has been expanding its production capacity in Vietnam and India in recent years, but most of its manufacturing still takes place in China. Now, Google has reportedly told its suppliers that it will be moving the production of all Pixel phones, watches and earbuds outside of China starting in 2027.
Nikkei Asia reported back in January that Google would develop and manufacture its Pixel 11 devices in Vietnam. The company had to invest in testing equipment and tooling machines, as well as to verify and fine-tune the production process in order to build its latest Pixel phones in Vietnam from scratch. It was reportedly that success, which gave Google the confidence that it could also build the production processes for its other devices in the country. Smartphone manufacturing, after all, is more complex than the production of earbuds and smartwatches.
A source told the publication that it will be easier for Google to move out of China than, say, Apple, because it doesn't officially sell Pixel devices in the country. In addition, its userbase for its phones is still currently pretty small, and the the company could tap into the smartphone supply chain ecosystem that Samsung had already established in Vietnam.
Google has also apparently told its suppliers that it's planning to raise Pixel phone shipments by 8 to 10 percent this year from 2025's 12 million units. The company is hoping that its phones will serve as a way to get more people to use Gemini's AI capabilities. In order to shield itself from the rising costs of memory components, Google has reportedly been bundling its orders for phone memory chips with chip orders for its cloud computing business.

Nearly one in three Indian women aged 15-49 years is now overweight or obese, up from one in four women five years ago, according to data released by the Central government. The latest National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) found that 30.7% of women aged 15-49 years were overweight or obese in 2023-24, compared with 24% in NFHS-5 (2019-21). Among men in the same age group, the proportion rose from 22.9% to 27.3%.
Speaking of the rising incidence of lifestyle-related disorders on fertility and pregnancy, which is prompting greater attention to health before conception, doctors and health practitioners are now increasingly focusing on the period before pregnancy, arguing that identifying and addressing health risks in both prospective parents could improve reproductive and pregnancy outcomes.
“The concept is not new to Ayurveda. The traditional system has described garbhadana samskara, a pre-conception regimen aimed at preparing prospective parents physically and mentally before conception. The approach is now being offered as a structured programme at the SDM College of Ayurveda and Hospital in Udupi, Karnataka, which has been providing pre-conception counselling and care to couples from different parts of south India,’’ Mamatha K.V., principal and senior obstetrician at the institution, said.
Describing this approach as the “conscious preparation for conception”, Dr. Mamatha said that the process involves assessment of the health of both partners, along with advice on diet, lifestyle, and other factors that may influence reproductive health. Pre-conception consultations can provide an opportunity to identify risks, review medicines, address nutritional deficiencies and encourage healthier lifestyles before pregnancy.
In Ayurveda, conception is described through four factors — ritu, the appropriate fertile period; kshetra, a healthy reproductive tract; beeja, the healthy sperm and ovum; and ambu, adequate nourishment. “Interventions are tailored around these factors, with dietary and lifestyle changes and, where considered appropriate, traditional therapies,’’ Shreyashri Suvarna, a physician at the hospital, said, adding that traditional interventions need to be individualised and clinically supervised.

Starsand Island Version 1.0 is now live, exiting its Early Access stage and giving you the full kit and caboodle of the farming simulator.

A New Multiplayer System
As revealed via the game’s Steam News Hub, Starsand Island 1.0 introduces the highly anticipated multiplayer system, allowing you to join your friends and other players and harvest resources throughout the Moonlit Forest.
The island host system lets you choose who can join and even set a password for a more personal farming experience.
You can complete requests with your friends together and explore different areas of the map. You can nurture your own little island, as each player keeps their individual island progress separate. - Crafting

- Livestock

Clearly, I'm on a breakfast kick.
Last week, I visited Cracker Barrel and IHOP to compare signature breakfasts for Business Insider. I concluded that both offered value, but in terms of taste, IHOP won most categories. That said, there was only one item per chain that I'd actually go back for.
I was content with my findings — until I read comments from BI readers singing Denny's praises, some of whom wanted to know my thoughts on the breakfast chain.
Honestly, I'd never been. And I was going to find out.
Denny's has been around for decades. This past year, it made headlines for going private and appointing a new CEO.
Denny's is a California-founded chain known for its classic American diner experience, select 24-hour locations, and all-day breakfast menu, specifically its trademarked Slam meals.
What started as a single doughnut shop in 1953 is now a massive operation with over 1,450 locations worldwide.
In late 2025, Denny's Corporation agreed to be acquired in a $620 million deal that took the company private in early 2026. The deal included both Denny's and Keke's Breakfast Cafe, the smaller chain Denny's acquired in 2022.
The company had been publicly traded for decades, and the shift followed struggles to boost sales and plans for widespread store closures.
A few months later, in April, Denny's appointed Christopher Bode, the chain's former president and COO, as president and CEO.
He stepped in to lead the brand's so-called transformation with "Project Grand Slam," a 24-month turnaround plan focused on pillars like remodels and culinary innovation.
"With Project Grand Slam, we aren't just changing the menu," Bode said in a press release. "We are changing our trajectory."
Time will tell if the rebranding project is, well, a grand slam. But in the meantime, I wanted to see if a chain I'd driven by a thousand times was actually worth a stop — especially when options like IHOP and Cracker Barrel are also on the table.
The Denny's I visited had subtle diner vibes.
When I hear "diner," I usually think of checkered floors, chrome finishes, bright-red accents, and vinyl booths.
Denny's had the old-school booths, but instead of tile, metal, and red, it had cherry-wood-looking floors and burgundy accents. Some elements, like the neon signs, still felt distinctly retro.
To me, it felt diner-adjacent, bridging retro and modern elements.
The decor didn't scream "diner" to me, but the menu sure did.
Opening my menu, I found an impressive lineup of pancakes, crepes, skillets, omelets, and the chain's iconic Grand Slam breakfast platters.
I felt Denny's breakfast section had more variety than Cracker Barrel's, which leans Southern and is missing some classics, but a little less than IHOP's, which has an especially impressive array of sweet options.
The chain also offered plenty of comfort meals like fried chicken, pot-roast sandwiches, and spaghetti and meatballs. However, I was here for breakfast.
I ordered coffee and a build-your-own Grand Slam.
To best match my orders at Cracker Barrel and IHOP, I built my own Grand Slam for $11.99.
It came with four items of my choosing, plus up to two additional items for a charge, ranging from $1.29 to $2.29 for more premium options.
I picked bacon strips, sausage links, scrambled eggs, and buttermilk pancakes, all served in pairs. I added grilled ham, a premium side, for an extra $2.29.
With my $3.29 coffee, the order came to $17.57.
Coffee started my meal off right.
I felt Cracker Barrel's coffee leaned weak and IHOP's basic, so I didn't anticipate much from Denny's.
Yet, it surprised me with a bold profile and a smooth, non-acidic finish. I appreciated the flavorful taste — and the bottomless refills.
Denny's pancakes really put the "cake" in pancakes.
The first thing I noticed about Denny's pancakes: They appeared even thicker than IHOP's (and therefore Cracker Barrel's, which were quite thin). Cutting in, they also seemed fluffier.
Denny's pancakes had a spongy-turned-pillowy bite that melted in my mouth, almost like actual cake. They even smelled like a birthday cake.
The buttermilk and vanilla flavors came through, and with understated sweetness, the texture shone. Denny's pancakes were easily the highlight of the meal, and given their volume, they certainly felt satisfying.
My scrambled eggs looked like an omelet.
Dense and firm, Denny's scrambled eggs lacked the soft, airy texture that typically defines the preparation. They made me wonder if my server accidentally brought out an omelet.
However, the eggs themselves were seasoned well, and the portion felt colossal compared to what I got at IHOP and Cracker Barrel. It seemed like way more than two eggs.
For crispy bacon, I'd go to Denny's.
Neither Cracker Barrel nor IHOP struck my fancy for crispy bacon. I finally found it at Denny's.
"Light" and "bacon" are rarely in the same sentence, but Denny's wispy strips delivered. Although thin, the middle remained tender and the edges had a pleasant crunch. It wasn't too salty, either.
The sausage links packed more flavor than value.
Breakfast sausage can disappear in the background, but Denny's links had an earthy, pine-like taste — what I imagined was sage.
Flavorful, yes, but the links looked like roughly half the size of IHOP's. Even though I enjoyed these flavors, I missed the larger-size links.
They seemed to contain about as much meat as the disappointing mini sausage patty I'd gotten with my breakfast combo at Cracker Barrel.
People who enjoy sweet ham would probably like Denny's.
With hints of sweetness, smoke, and barbecue spice, Denny's grilled ham slice had a unique profile. Sweetness took center stage, as though the slice had been dipped in maple syrup. Even though I prefer savory ham, I could appreciate the distinctive flavor.
I also found it more tender than Cracker Barrel's and more memorable than IHOP's.
The substantial weight made it worth an extra charge, though $2.29 felt a little high for one piece of meat.
Realizing I could get one more add-on with my meal, I tried the hash browns.
My Denny's experience wouldn't be complete without hash browns, and since they were considered my second add-on, they cost me only $1.29.
With six approvals in the taste department, I assumed Denny's hash browns would follow suit. I stood corrected.
Comparatively, Cracker Barrel's hash-brown casserole blew me away — so much so that I would go back for that side alone. IHOP's hash browns were just OK.
Denny's were stringy, greasy, and firm, to the point I wondered if they were undercooked. The heaping portion was generous, but I could barely eat two bites. I may have just gotten a bad batch.
Ultimately, Denny's had the best chain breakfast so far — especially when it comes to pancakes.
With hash browns, my order totaled $18.86 before tax and tip. The same seven items cost $16.88 at Cracker Barrel and $18.58 at IHOP, so Denny's came out pricier than both.
All three chains felt like a solid value for the amount of food I got, but in my opinion, Denny's provided the biggest bang for my buck.
With relatively similar prices, value comes down to taste, variety, and portion size.
Taste is subjective, of course, but for this particular meal, Denny's did it for me. All but one item was yummy enough to order again, something I couldn't say the same about either of the other chains.
I also appreciated the build-your-own Grand Slam's customizability. I had 13 items to choose from, including egg whites, turkey bacon, buttermilk biscuits, and seasonal fruit — many of which I'd be interested in trying next time.
Above all else, aside from Denny's sausages, everything else seemed either equal or larger in size than what I got at Cracker Barrel and IHOP.
In my comparison of Cracker Barrel and IHOP, I noted that I'd only go back for hash-brown casserole and pancakes, respectively. I stand by Cracker Barrel for crispy spuds, but for pancakes, there's a new winner in my book.
I'd choose Denny's fluffy flapjacks any day of the week.
Denny's declined to comment.
Read my full IHOP and Cracker Barrel comparison here — and let me know which chain's breakfast I should try next.

China’s economy is showing signs of extending a slowdown with a slump in industrial output and retail sales in July, adding to pressure on Beijing to intervene with measures to support activity.
After the world’s second largest economy posted one of its lowest quarterly growth readings on record in the three months to June, the latest figures suggest it continued to falter in July.
Factory output grew 4.5% from a year earlier last month, compared with 5.3% in June, official figures from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Monday, missing a Reuters poll forecast for 4.8% growth.
Separate figures showed retail sales grew 0.6%, a slowdown from a 1% rise in June despite summer holiday tourism spending. Forecasters had predicted 1.5%.
The NBS said extreme weather, including high temperatures and heavy rainfall, had disrupted market supply and demand.
The latest snapshot, however is likely to increase pressure on policymakers to accelerate plans for tax and spending measures to support activity.
China’s premier, Li Qiang, suggested on Monday that efforts to bolster overseas demand for goods could be used to make up for weak domestic demand.
“Currently, the problem of insufficient domestic demand remains prominent, some industries and enterprises are facing increasing difficulties, and uncertainties in external environment are rising,” Li told a meeting of China’s state council, according to the state news agency, Xinhua.
“We should actively stabilise external demand, expand mutually beneficial international economic and trade cooperation and promote balanced trade development.”
Analysts say they expect stronger growth rates later this year, supported by spending measures from Beijing to increase activity.
“The silver lining is that the boost to manufacturing activity from AI capex [capital expenditure] continued to build, and that the wider weakness partly reflects temporary disruptions from recent typhoons,” said Julian Evans-Pritchard, the head of China economics at the consultancy Capital Economics.
“We still expect a modest uptick in growth over the rest of the year, supported by fiscal loosening.”
The latest snapshot comes after China posted a worse-than-expected annualised growth rate of 4.3% in the three months to June, one of its lowest quarterly readings on record.
The rate, which came in under the government’s target of 4.5% to 5%, was one of the weakest since Beijing began reporting official quarterly GDP data in the early 1990s.

Thailand has a gun problem - 10 million of them
- Published
Just three days after a 14-year-old opened fire at his school, killing eight people before shooting himself, another incident in the same province illustrated even more starkly Thailand's troubled relationship with guns.
Chalong Riewrang, a 71-year-old former politician, went into the local administration office to discuss a large sum of money he says he was owed by the administration chief, Thongchai Yenprasert, a man he called his friend.
The conversation ended abruptly with Chalong pulling out a gun and firing four shots through the window of Thongchai's car, hitting him and his driver. Thongchai later died from his wounds.
Chalong then left the scene, and phoned a startled journalist he knew who was in the middle of a live broadcast on YouTube, to tell her what had happened.
After the police intercepted him and took him to the station, he was allowed to speak to reporters, casually smoking a cigarette and seemingly unperturbed by what he had done.
He explained that he had "not intended to shoot his friend", but opened fire when the driver also pulled a gun. The police did find two guns in the car, but said they were not in a state where they could have been fired.
This was not the only gun fatality in Thailand on that day. In Prachinburi, east of Bangkok, a police sergeant shot his wife in the head while arguing with her as she was driving their car to pick up their young son. The car crashed and the sergeant then shot himself in the head. His wife died in hospital.
There were probably other gun deaths that day which were not reported by the media.
The Thai police do not keep their own tally, but in recent years the number of gun deaths every year is estimated to range between 2,000 and 3,000. In Britain, which has a similar population, the number is less than 50.
Guns are sometimes used in robberies, and for a relatively modest fee you can hire a hitman in Thailand to kill someone for you. But the typical gun death occurs during domestic disputes, financial disagreements, or in bar brawls fuelled by alcohol.
Thailand has more than 10 million civilian-owned guns in circulation - 4 million of those unlicensed. So that means minor altercations over trivial issues can suddenly turn lethal.
"It's very unfortunate that Thailand has a very high tolerance for violence," says Boonwara Sumano at the Thailand Development Research Institute.
"Guns are seen as a status symbol, and there are so many ways that civilians can get them. Also, showing strength, wielding power, is seen as the right thing to do in Thai society. So, when you have a norm that promotes the possession of weapons to show your strength, and access to those weapons, this is the result."
At first sight Thailand appears to have quite strict gun regulations. Anyone wishing to buy a gun must first apply for a purchase permit, then, once they have bought it, apply for a second possession permit. If they wish to carry the gun outside their homes they then need a third permit. Imported guns – most of them - are very expensive.
But there are huge loopholes. The possession permits are valid for the lifetime of the holder. There is no requirement for mental health screening. And there are no checks on how safely guns are stored. For instance, the boy who carried out the latest school shooting was able to get hold of his grandfather's legally owned gun and large quantities of ammunition.
There is also a government scheme under which police officers and other officials can buy guns at steeply discounted prices.
Around 200,000 guns have been imported every year, mostly from the US, under the scheme, which started in 2009.
They can then be resold after five years, which has become a lucrative business.
The scheme has been investigated several times over alleged corruption. Together with weapons made locally by unlicensed gunmakers it is believed to be the source of many black market guns in Thailand.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has ordered immediate measures to tighten gun control, suspending the discount purchase scheme and the issuing of all purchase licences.
He is talking about limiting the validity of possession permits, and a possible amnesty to encourage those with unlicensed guns to hand them in.
He has asked parliament to work on a new law, and vowed severe penalties for those who break the rules.
But we have been here before.
After the massacre of children and teachers by a former police officer at a nursery in 2022, and then after a shooting by another 14-year-old boy at Bangkok's most popular shopping mall in 2023, Anutin, then the interior minister, ordered similar measures.
The discount scheme was also suspended back then, but almost immediately reinstated. The carrying of firearms by anyone not on official duty was banned after another school shooting in February this year.
The problem is not just regulation. The sheer number of guns in circulation, endemic corruption, lax enforcement of laws in all walks of life, the glorification of guns and a decades-long military culture are all contributing factors.
In the most recent asset declarations by government ministers more than a dozen owned guns: the justice minister owns 10, the minister for the environment and natural resources said he had 12, and one female MP has declared ownership of 48 guns.
Boonwara Sumano also highlights the pervasive influence of the military in Thailand, even when it is not actually running the country, which it has done for most of its modern history.
"If you notice every Children's Day in Thailand, instead of taking children to a museum or park, many families take their children to an army or air force base to see the weapons, take photos holding guns, this kind of thing.
"It's in the culture. You see big men in the military looking so powerful, they kind of make you want to become one of them," she told the BBC.
Thailand is an outlier in this region.
Compared to Thailand's 10 million, Indonesia has only 82,000 civilian-owned guns, with a population four times larger. In Malaysia the number is 107,000, and deaths from gunshots are rare.
The Philippines is the only other country with a similar gun-culture and comparable levels of gun crime.
Gun enthusiasts in Thailand now worry that the government will react to public anxiety over the latest attacks by making even responsible gun ownership much harder.
Yod, a 53-year-old businessman, told the BBC he viewed his collection of more than 70 guns more as luxurious toys – he said he had never fired most of them.
"Most of the gun crimes in this country are carried out by illegal weapons. New measures to control legally owned guns are not the right solution. There are blank guns and spare parts which can be assembled as real guns being imported legally into the country. Why hasn't that been chased up?"
Sathit, a shop-owner with more than 40 guns in his collection, cited the weakness of law enforcement in Thailand as his reason for arming himself.
"Look around this country nowadays. There are crimes every day. It is not safe. Drugs are rampant. People need to protect themselves because there are not enough police officers. People should have access to guns to survive, for their own safety."
As he waited to be charged for carrying out a killing he had apparently not even thought about when he walked into the local administration office, Chalong Riewrang, a powerful local figure accustomed to getting his own way, ruminated to reporters on his unforeseen situation.
"I can't believe I'm in this position, sitting here. Throughout my life, I have never had to come to a police station."
At one time, according to the police, he had possessed permits for nine guns, but in recent years had reduced that to just one. One gun, it turned out, was enough to end the life of his friend, and turn his upside down.

'Will form high-powered panel': SC on Delhi Police 'excesses' against student protesters
Edited by: Karan Manral / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 18, 2026, 15:21 IST

Student protest in Jantar Mantar ( File Image)
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday said it would constitute a high-powered committee to examine allegations of police excesses during recent student protests in Delhi.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana will pass the order on Wednesday after receiving suggestions from the parties on other members to be included in the panel.The bench further stated it will direct the authorities to hand over video footage and CCTV recordings of the violence during the July 20 Parliament march in Delhi to the committee for examination.
The panel will also examine complaints and allegations made by female protesters who were reportedly targeted during the march and in other areas.During the hearing, the bench asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, to provide details of FIRs registered against student protesters that could be quashed, indicating that the court may exercise its plenary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution.“It is the life of students, which is at stake. We have to consider this. They have a future ahead. They have the right to protest under Article 19,” the bench told a counsel opposing the quashing of cases against student protesters without them tendering an apology.
On August 3, the Supreme Court clarified that the expression “criminal antecedents” in its order on the release of student protesters referred only to those involved in grave and heinous offences.
It also clarified that states could close or withdraw FIRs against other students in accordance with the law.The clarification came after the Centre submitted that it was “serious” about not pursuing FIRs against students who participated in demonstrations over the NEET examination paper leak, including the July 20 Parliament march in Delhi, provided they did not have criminal antecedents.The top court had earlier observed that police excesses or a “lathi charge” could not be justified merely because there was an agitation and underlined that the right to peaceful protest was “absolutely guaranteed”.The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led march on July 20 in Delhi witnessed clashes between protesters and security personnel, who used lathis and teargas shells to disperse crowds attempting to move towards Parliament.(With PTI inputs)

TOKYO – The Asian Games begin in Japan in a month’s time featuring teenage prodigies, more athletes than the Olympics and a cruise ship that will house competitors in the middle of typhoon season.
About 15,000 competitors and officials are expected at the event, which takes place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from Sept. 19 to Oct. 4.
Among those in action will be Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala and a pair of world-class talents in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.
Organizers hope the athletes will have a “unique experience” staying in accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to standard hotel rooms.
Kazuhiro Yagi, vice-secretary general of the Aichi-Nagoya Games organizing committee, said, “it feels like the Games are right around the corner.”
“The final stages of preparation are now upon us,” he said.
“We will continue working as one right until the last moment and we hope that people from all over Asia, not just Japan, will enjoy the event.”
Organizers have opted for temporary athlete accommodation to cut costs, hiring the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena for the event.
Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on the ship, which features 571 cabins, seven swimming pools, eight restaurants and nine bars.
Officials are confident that the plan will not be disrupted by Japan’s typhoon season, which is usually in full swing in September-October.
A further 2,000 athletes and officials will stay in wooden shipping container-style huts in Nagoya’s Garden Pier area while the rest will stay in hotels.
That includes in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events will take place.
“For the athletes the accommodation is a place to relax and socialise with their fellow competitors,” said Yagi.
“To ensure that all athletes can enjoy a comfortable stay and deliver their best performance, preparations for accommodation are entering their final stage.”
Eala will be among the most prominent athletes competing in Nagoya, and the 21-year-old will be looking to continue her rapid rise in women’s tennis.
The world number 20 became the first player from the Philippines to win a WTA title when she triumphed at the Washington Open earlier this month.
She is hot property in her home country, sparking a rush of interest in tennis and inspiring youngsters to take up the sport.
Sooryavanshi will also turn heads after announcing himself as a major new talent in world cricket.
The gifted teenager became the youngest cricketer to represent India last month when he debuted in a Twenty20 match against England.
Sooryavanshi will be hoping to win gold at Japan’s newly built cricket ground, where defending champions India could face arch-rivals Pakistan in the men’s final.
Swimmer Yu has also made a name for herself with her astonishing progress in the pool, setting a new women’s 200m individual medley Asian record last year.
Yu, who turns 14 in October, will be part of a Chinese team that will again look to top the medals table after dominating on home soil at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023.
China won a record 201 golds, almost four times as many as second-place Japan.
As always at the Asian Games, traditional sports like athletics, swimming and football sit side by side with more local disciplines such as kabaddi, sepak takraw and wushu.
New events at the 20th edition of the Games include mixed martial arts, padel, teqball and virtual taekwondo.
Esports returns after a hugely successful debut in Hangzhou, with Nagoya organizers saying they hope to inspire elderly people to keep their minds sharp by picking up a controller.
With the Asian Games returning to Japan for the first time since 1994, the organizing committee’s Yagi said the atmosphere was “gradually becoming palpable.”
“We hope to move you and excite you, and to showcase the wonder of sport,” he said.

Raids create fear, food safety law prioritises reform: Ex-Maharashtra FDA chief
Zagade said the law laid down a graded process under which an improvement notice should first be issued to a non-compliant establishment. Its licence should be suspended only if it fails to make the required changes, he added.
Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe’s “Safe Food, Safe Maharashtra” campaign has drawn attention to raids that exposed alleged hygiene violations at restaurants and other food establishments across the state.
The campaign, however, has also faced criticism from some quarters over what they describe as a “shoot first, talk later” approach.
Amid the continuing crackdown, former IAS officer Mahesh Zagade, who served as Maharashtra FDA commissioner between 2011 and 2014, has questioned the emphasis on raids and licence suspensions. Speaking to India Today, he said the law focused on improving food standards rather than creating fear among businesses.
LAW FOCUSES ON IMPROVEMENT, NOT RAIDS
Zagade said the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, had focused heavily on raids to curb adulteration, a system that he claimed also enabled extortion by some officials.
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, marked a shift towards food quality and preventive action, he said.
“Even if you take action against a defaulter, the consumer may already have consumed the unhealthy product. Therefore, the focus should be on improvement,” Zagade said.
Recalling his tenure, he said the FDA had avoided excessive publicity and concentrated on helping establishments improve their practices.
“We did not publicise our work much, but we focused on improvements, which produced good results. Food vendors at Juhu Chowpatty made significant improvements,” he said.
‘RAIDS CREATE FEAR, NOT CHANGE’
Zagade said the law laid down a graded process under which an improvement notice should first be issued to a non-compliant establishment. Its licence should be suspended only if it fails to make the required changes, he added.
He argued that a campaign centred on raids and licence suspensions could create two misleading impressions.
“First, people may assume that no work was being done earlier and that unhygienic food is being served everywhere. The fact is that inspections and licence suspensions take place regularly. We should not defame local businesses,” he said.
Second, Zagade warned that widespread fear among business owners could create opportunities for extortion and impersonation.
“Some people may pose as FDA officials and cheat businesses. Officials may also go overboard and engage in illegal activities,” he said.
COURT ORDER SHOWS NEED TO ‘REORIENT’
Zagade also referred to an adverse court ruling against the FDA in a Pune case, in which the department was reportedly fined Rs 5 lakh for continuing the suspension of an establishment’s licence despite a compliance report of 98 per cent.
“During my tenure, many improvement notices were issued and licences were suspended in some cases, but there was no adverse court ruling,” he said.
The retired IAS official added that the Pune case suggests that the FDA needs to reorient its approach.
NOTICES TO ACTORS OVER PAN MASALA ADS
The former FDA commissioner also responded to notices issued to three actors over advertisements for Vimal Elaichi.
Zagade said tobacco, pan masala and scented supari had been banned during his tenure and that misleading advertisements should attract action under Section 53 of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
He, however, said enforcement should not be limited to the celebrities appearing in such advertisements.
“I hope action has also been taken against the company that manufactures the product. If a person is shot, you punish the shooter, not the weapon. Action should therefore be taken against those who make and broadcast misleading advertisements,” Zagade said.
He recalled a case from his tenure involving a well-known actor who endorsed a product claiming to cure knee pain.
“I banned the product. The actor approached me and asked what would happen to him. I told him my team would decide that, but the product had been banned. None of this appeared in the media,” he said.
‘LAW IS NOT MEANT TO SHUT HOTELS’
Zagade stressed that while people consume some food at restaurants and roadside outlets, most meals are prepared and eaten in homes. Improving household food safety was therefore equally important, he said.
“If I prepare food at home and find cockroaches in the kitchen, will I shut down my kitchen? I will remove the pests and improve hygiene,” he said.
He added that the law was intended not to shut down five-star hotels but to improve public health, particularly among the most vulnerable sections.

Luma Reader by TechPP turns long webpages into short, animated paragraphs for a cleaner and more engaging reading experience. It removes distractions, saves highlights, remembers your progress, supports dark mode and font controls, and works on desktop and mobile browsers.
There are hundreds of reader apps and extensions available for free. But the idea behind our extension is not just offering a clean and distraction-free reading experience but also making reading text more immersive, especially in an era where people prefer watching videos over reading text.
Thanks to short-form content, especially platforms like YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, users’ attention span has reduced drastically. It is even affecting the longer video format, and text is currently the least preferred way of consumption for most people.
Short-form text is currently the trending format, thanks to AI tools; however, similar to short videos, most short-form answers don’t offer the full context, depth, and meaning of the information.
So we built a simple motion-reader extension to enhance the reading experience. The extension not only strips all unwanted content from the web page but also displays animated text, making the reading experience more immersive and visually appealing while keeping it short and simple. It strips out long text from any webpage and converts it into short, interactive, readable content.
The extension is also free to download. You can get it from here, and at the end of this post is a detailed guide on how to install and use it on Google Chrome on desktop and mobile browsers. The process is very similar for other browsers too.
Here are five reasons why you should use our Luma Reader by TechPP extension:
Table of Contents
Read With Short Motion Paragraphs
The biggest reason why people prefer short-form content is that it is easy to grasp and also visually appealing. That’s not the case with text. Most websites, especially news and blog sites, still use long reading paragraphs, which are immediately a red flag for many people.
In addition to that, many webpages have other distracting elements that can hinder the user’s reading experience. To make text easy to read, our extension visually presents the text, strips out all the unwanted content on a web page, and gives you simple, short paragraphs.
Even if the web page consists of longer paragraphs, our extension converts text into smaller interactive sentences (max of two or three) to make it easy to read.
Once you finish reading the current sentences, you can swipe up for the new text, or swipe down if you want to read the previous text. This way, you won’t feel overwhelmed by the amount of text.
This short and simple, guided, interactive reading experience is significantly better and less mentally demanding, and breaks the information into bits that are easier to read.

We also added the ability to highlight text and save it permanently. It works just like any other text annotation tool: you can simply long-press on any text and click the highlight option. All the text highlights will be permanently saved on your browser storage unless you manually delete the browser data. You can revisit these highlights at any time.
Continue Reading Where You Left Off
The USP of our Luma Reader extension is the ability to read from where you left off. Most reader extensions just strip the web elements. Since ours uses a unique approach of showing the small text in motion animations, it is important to let users read where they left off instead of scrolling from the beginning. Our extension remembers where you left off and resumes from there.
Read Comfortably With Dark Mode
Most people prefer reading text in dark mode. If you are one of them, our Luma Reader extension supports dark mode too. You can simply enable it from the top toolbar. You can also adjust different levels based on your preference.

Why has Salah chosen to join Trabzonspor?
- Published
After months of speculation, Mohamed Salah's next destination has finally been confirmed.
The Liverpool legend agreed a two-year deal, external with Turkish side Trabzonspor on Thursday following the expiry of his contract at Anfield, bringing an end to one of the most successful careers in Premier League history.
The move has surprised many.
For years, Saudi Pro League clubs pursued Salah, while Major League Soccer was also viewed as a realistic destination for one of world football's biggest stars. Instead, the 34-year-old has remained in Europe by joining Trabzonspor, a club better known for upsetting Turkey's established order than dominating it.
So why has Salah chosen Trabzonspor, and what can both player and club expect from one another?
Staying in Europe remained the priority
Money alone does not explain Salah's decision. Saudi Arabian clubs had long identified the Egyptian as one of their priority targets, with Al-Ittihad even making a late approach, while Sporting Kansas City were among the MLS clubs interested in bringing him to the United States.
Both destinations could have offered enormous monetary rewards. Instead, Salah opted to stick with European football.
He will be very well paid in Turkey. In a posting to the Turkish stock exchange, Trabzonspor confirmed he will be paid £14.5m per season and will receive a 20% share of revenue from Salah-branded merchandise.
Trabzonspor finished third in last season's Super Lig and will compete in this month's Europa League play-offs. Victory over two legs would see them qualify for the league phase, while defeat would send them into the Conference League.
For a player who helped Egypt reach the knockout stages of this summer's World Cup and produced one of the finest campaigns of his career in 2024-25, continuing to compete in Uefa competition appears to have carried significant weight.
Why Trabzonspor?
If Salah was determined to stay in Europe, Trabzonspor might not have been the obvious choice.
Turkey's traditional powerhouses are Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas, with most of the country's biggest-name arrivals historically choosing one of the Istanbul giants.
Besiktas did attempt to sign Salah before negotiations collapsed over the financial structure of the deal, opening the door for Trabzonspor.
Although they lack the global profile of Turkey's biggest clubs, Trabzonspor are far from outsiders.
They are seven-time Turkish champions, won the Super Lig as recently as 2021-22 and lifted last season's Turkish Cup.
Fatih Tekke's side also finished third in the league, earning another opportunity to qualify for European competition.
Salah instantly becomes the biggest signing in the club's history. The excitement surrounding his arrival underlined that status as hundreds of supporters gathered to welcome him before he travelled on to Trabzon.
Former Scotland midfielder Ryan Jack, who won the Scottish Premiership with Rangers in 2021, has spent the last two seasons playing in Turkey. He was not surprised by the scenes.
"That's one thing about Turkish football - the fans are incredibly passionate," he told BBC Sport. "The big clubs have huge support and they really get behind their teams."
During his unveiling, he briefly wore a symbolic number 61 shirt in tribute to the city, with the number representing Trabzon's vehicle registration code and holding special significance among supporters, who traditionally celebrate the 61st minute of matches.
However, for the 2026-27 season, Salah will wear the number 10 shirt after requesting the number he also wears for Egypt. Team-mate Ernest Muci agreed to relinquish the jersey as a gesture of respect for the club's marquee signing.
Why Turkey continues to attract elite players
Salah's move is the latest sign of Turkish football's growing appeal to established stars.
Victor Osimhen, Leroy Sane, Ilkay Gundogan, Nathan Ake and Leandro Trossard are among the high-profile names now playing in the Super Lig, while Andre Onana, Ruslan Malinovskyi and Stefan Savic are already part of Trabzonspor's squad.
Last summer, the Super Lig recorded the third-highest net transfer spend in world football behind only the Premier League and Saudi Pro League, highlighting the league's increasing ambition.
The economics behind that spending are unusual.
Turkey's biggest clubs generate substantial income in euros through Uefa competition while many domestic operating costs remain in Turkish lira.
The country's prolonged period of high inflation has also reduced the relative value of existing domestic debt, giving clubs greater flexibility than might initially appear.
Financially, Trabzonspor were therefore able to present Salah with an attractive package.
Reports in Turkey say he has signed a two-year contract until June 2028 worth around £7.3m per season, below the salary he could reportedly have earned in Saudi Arabia, with additional bonuses and a share of merchandise revenue linked to his name.
The result is a league capable of offering competitive salaries, passionate fanbases and European football to players entering the latter stages of their careers.
Jack believes the competition's profile is continuing to rise.
"The league is getting stronger every year and you're seeing more and more big names joining," he said.
"Salah is probably the biggest name to move to Turkey in recent years. It shows the league is growing and it might persuade other top players to consider going there. There are great stadiums, great cities and it's a competitive league."
His own experience reinforced that impression.
"I loved it," Jack added. "Everyone helps you settle in and the people are really friendly. When foreign players arrive, the clubs do everything they can to help them."
Is the standard high enough?
Despite attracting recognisable names, the Super Lig is some way below Europe's elite competitions.
Opta currently ranks it as the 14th strongest domestic league in world football, behind top-flights in countries such as Denmark, Poland and even England's Championship.
Turkish clubs have also found sustained European success difficult to achieve.
Since Galatasaray won the Uefa Cup in 2000, only one Turkish side has reached the semi-finals of a major Uefa competition, illustrating the gap that still exists between Turkey's biggest clubs and Europe's established powers.
For Salah, however, the move represents a compromise. Rather than stepping away from European football he will continue playing continental competition while competing in one of the most fervent environments.
Can Salah still perform at the highest level?
Age suggests Salah is entering the twilight of his career, but there is evidence he still has plenty to offer.
He inspired Egypt to the knockout stages of the 2026 World Cup, contributing one goal and two assists in five appearances.
His final season at Liverpool proved more difficult as the defending Premier League champions slipped to fifth place amid a disappointing campaign.
Salah scored 12 goals across all competitions after falling out of favour under Arne Slot.
Only a year earlier, he had delivered one of the best individual campaigns of his career, scoring 34 goals and registering 23 assists in all competitions as Liverpool lifted the Premier League title.
Even allowing for his decline last season, few players arriving in Turkey possess anything close to Salah's pedigree.
Trabzonspor are expected to build their attack around him immediately.
Fatih Tekke's side typically operate in a 4-2-3-1, with Salah expected to occupy his familiar position on the right wing, cutting inside onto his stronger left foot in the role that made him one of Europe's most prolific forwards.
Tekke can also switch to a 4-3-3 without majorly altering Salah's responsibilities, leaving the Egyptian as the focal point of the club's attacking threat.
His competitive debut could come on 15 August when Trabzonspor open their Super Lig campaign away to Kasimpasa, before attention quickly turns to a Europa League play-off against either Hungary's Ferencvaros or Poland's Gornik Zabrze.
A statement signing
For Trabzonspor, the transfer extends far beyond what Salah might produce on the pitch.
His arrival immediately raises the club's global profile, boosts commercial opportunities and provides one of the most marketable footballers of the modern era.
Jack also believes Salah's arrival will increase international interest in the Turkish game.
"I think Liverpool fans, and people who love watching Salah, will definitely take notice and start following the league," he said.
"When I moved there, my family and friends started watching games because they didn't really know much about Turkish football before. Salah's move will make people sit up and watch more of the league."
Meanwhile, for Salah, the move offers something perhaps more valuable than another lucrative contract.
He remains in Europe, has the chance to compete for domestic honours and European football, and becomes the undisputed figurehead of one of Turkey's most historic clubs.
It may not have been the destination many expected, but for both player and club, Trabzonspor represents an opportunity to begin an ambitious new chapter.

The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations (PM CARES) Fund saw the donations it received grow by 592% in 2024-25 to nearly ₹480 crore, as per the audited financial statements for 2023-24 and 2024-25, which it made available on Tuesday (August 18, 2026) after having failed to upload the annual disclosure documents since 2022-23.
The Hindu had highlighted the lapse on August 8.
The PM CARES Fund, a public charitable trust established in March 2020 to support relief efforts during public health emergencies and other disasters, is chaired by the Prime Minister and funded entirely through voluntary contributions, as per information released by the Central government.
Barely any spending
Reacting to the belated disclosure, Anjali Bhardwaj, co-convenor of the National Campaign for People’s Right to Information (NCPRI), said in her social media post: “Finally the audit statement of PM CARES Fund for 2024-25 has been made public! Key highlights — utilised only 0.01% of available ₹8,452 crore!”
Ms. Bhardwaj was referring to the fact that while the Fund received a total income — including net donations, interest on bank deposits and fixed deposits, and refunds from implementing agencies — of ₹1,279.9 crore in 2024-25, it spent ₹87.85 lakh or 0.1% of that amount that year and 0.01% of the fund’s closing balance.
Taken together, from its start in March 2020 until March 31, 2025, the PM CARES Fund has spent less than one-fifth (18.7%) of what it has received as income.
High balances, opaque filings
As a result of low spending, the closing balance of the Fund has grown substantially over the years. The closing balance of the Fund stood at ₹8,452.06 crore in 2024-25, which is 17.8% higher than at the end of the previous year.
“Why is the PM CARES Fund keeping such large sums of money idle,” Ms. Bhardwaj further asked. She also pointed out that while ₹324 crore had been refunded by implementing agencies in 2024-25, no information had been provided on what these payments were for, why they were refunded, or which agency refunded them.
“Were refunds done to evade accountability for faulty equipment?” she said. “Also, why have accompanying notes to the audit report not been uploaded?”
Lack of accountability
Ms. Bhardwaj added that a fund set up to help citizens during disasters, which has accumulated thousands of crores, including from foreign sources, is “shrouded in secrecy”.
“Still no information available on sources of funds,” she said. “The PM CARES Fund continues to evade public scrutiny by refusing to submit itself to the RTI Act.”
Activists had previously questioned the absence of publicly available audit statements after FY 2022-23, saying this raised concerns about the transparency of the PM CARES Fund, which had been announced three days before the close of the 2019-20 financial year through a Central government communication.
They maintained that several thousand crore rupees were contributed under the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) provisions by public sector undertakings, which is public money. The fund was presented as having been set up by the Central Government, making it appear to be a public authority. Government employees also contributed from their salaries.
The Prime Minister chairs the fund in his ex-officio capacity and Union Cabinet Ministers are its trustees.
“However, when information regarding the funds collected and spent was sought, the government maintained that the trust is not a public authority under the RTI Act,” Ms. Bhardwaj had told The Hindu. “The Ministry of Corporate Affairs also retrospectively amended the relevant rules under the Companies Act. At present, PM CARES remains outside the ambit of the RTI Act, parliamentary scrutiny and audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG).”

A hot day could be expected to have an extra four hours of extreme heat by the end of the century if the planet continues to warm under a high-emissions scenario, a study has found.
Researchers, including those from China's Sun Yat-sen University and Southern Marine Science and Engineering Guangdong Laboratory, also projected that days not categorised as 'hot days' -- having a heat exceeding 90 per cent of those on previously measured days -- could potentially gain a further three hot hours.
Low and middle-income countries are likely to be the worst hit, findings published in the journal Nature Climate Change show.
Extreme heat events are typically assessed using daily mean average, maximum, or minimum temperatures. However, the measures can neglect shorter but potentially important periods of extreme heat, the researchers said.
The modelling study shows that hourly assessments can capture heat exposure overlooked by daily metrics and could support a more effective heat risk management and public health planning, they said.
Global hourly data, combining weather observations and model estimates during 1981-2023 and coupled with future climate projections to the end of the 21st century, was analysed.
Land areas around the world experience an average of approximately 269 hours of extreme heat each summer, the analysis found.
An hourly heat event was defined as temperature exceeding 90 per cent of previous measurements of that hour during the baseline of 1981-2010.
More than 80% of the world's land area showed an increase in heat, with an average of 62 additional hours per decade of extreme heat between 1981 and 2023 -- 28 per cent of the events were also found to occur on days not identified as heat extremes by daily metrics.
"HHEs (hourly heat extremes) are emerging worldwide and exhibit marked unequal exposure across regions and generations," the authors wrote.
By late century, hourly heat extreme events could be expected to increase fourfold with a sixfold increase in population exposed to such instances under a high-emissions scenario, they found.
"Each hot day will gain about four hot hours, and a further three hot hours will occur on non-hot days, which daily metrics overlook," they wrote.
Low and middle-income countries were found to account for more than three-quarters of both current and projected heat exposure and face the largest increases in lifetime exposure across generations.
The researchers said future research should focus on mechanisms causing hourly heat extremes, such as heat bursts or flash heat events.
An improved understanding of short-term heat events on an hourly scale could improve early warning systems, potential health risk assessments, and adaptation to a warming climate, they said.

The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.
Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.
On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.
A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”
Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.
The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.
On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.
But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.
The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.
Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson is appealing - here's what you need to know
- Published
A year after her blockbuster trial, Australia's notorious mushroom murderer is facing court again, in a bid to overturn her conviction.
Erin Patterson was jailed for life last September for murdering three relatives and trying to kill another with a toxic mushroom meal she served at her home in Leongatha, Victoria, in 2023.
But the 51-year-old says she did not receive a fair trial, citing problems with evidence, the actions of the prosecution, and an unusual mishap with the jury while they deliberated on their verdicts.
At the same time that Erin Patterson's case is heard, prosecutors will also be appealing her sentence. The judge said Patterson could apply for parole after 33 years, but the prosecution says that's "manifestly inadequate" and the triple murderer should never be freed.
What did Erin Patterson do?
Patterson killed her in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, after serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms at her home in rural Victoria in 2023.
Heather's husband, Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, survived the lunch after weeks in hospital and still has ongoing health issues related to the poisoning.
Patterson's estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.
After the trial, it was revealed that he had become so violently ill after eating several of her meals in the past that he had been in a coma, a large part of his bowel had been surgically removed, and his family were told to say goodbye to him twice as he was not expected to survive his ailments.
Erin Patterson maintained throughout the trial that she never meant to kill her relatives - that it was all a terrible accident, and her lies and attempts to dispose of evidence in the aftermath of the lunch were because she was panicking she would be blamed for the deaths.
What is Patterson arguing?
Patterson won't be attending the appeal in person. She's chosen to appear via video link from Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, the maximum security prison on the outskirts of Melbourne where she's serving her sentence.
Last November, her legal team filed a three-page document outlining the arguments they plan to make in an effort to overturn her conviction.
There are seven grounds for this appeal, which will be heard by three judges.
Firstly, there are bits of evidence Patterson's lawyers say the jurors should never have seen: for example, mobile phone tracking data that indicated she'd travelled to places where death cap mushrooms were recently spotted.
Her lawyers also argue that evidence from "Facebook friends" should not have been allowed. That included online messages in which she ranted about her in-laws as well as her estranged husband Simon Patterson, at one point calling him a "deadbeat".
All that evidence, Patterson's team says, was not relevant and prejudicial, causing a substantial miscarriage of justice.
But her lawyers also argue that other pieces of evidence would have helped Patterson in court. Photos and images relating to her hobby as a long-time mushroom forager - and supporting their argument that the deaths were a tragic accident - had been wrongly excluded, the defence says.
Then there are their issues with the prosecution. Patterson's team say they were inconsistent about a motive, starting the trial by saying they wouldn't argue a particular motive, but ending it by implying there was one.
They also criticise the five days Patterson was cross-examined by barrister Nannette Rogers. At times it felt tense witnessing the two sparring in the courtroom, with Rogers accusing her of repeatedly lying. Patterson argues it was "unfair and oppressive".
But the most intriguing aspect of the appeal document submitted by Erin Patterson's lawyers relates to the jury deliberations.
Because there was so much hype around the case, there were steps taken throughout the trial to ensure the jury wasn't influenced by friends, family or the media. When they began deliberating, they had to stay in supervised accommodation, with little to no contact with the outside world, until they reached a decision.
But according to Patterson's lawyers, a "fundamental irregularity" occurred which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts.
It turns out that room shortages caused by the media frenzy in the regional towns around the courthouse meant the jury wound up sharing a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.
The jury had a whole hotel floor to themselves, and the judge at the time said there was no evidence they had any interaction with anyone linked to the case.
Patterson's team didn't raise any concerns during the trial, but in their appeal filing said: "[This] requires the quashing of the convictions and an order for a re-trial so that justice cannot only be done but be seen to be done."
What is the prosecution saying?
The Department of Public Prosecutions (DPP) is appealing over the length of Patterson's sentence.
Justice Christopher Beale last year agreed that Patterson's crimes were the worst of their kind, but said his decision to allow parole after 33 years was influenced by the "harsh prison conditions" she faced.
He noted that she'd already spent 15 months in solitary confinement at the time of her sentencing. In solitary confinement, prisoners cannot mix and meals are delivered via a small opening in the cell door.
For her own safety, he added, there was a "substantial chance" that she would be held in an isolation wing "for years to come" because of the notoriety of her case.
What happens next?
The outcome of the appeal will not be known immediately after these hearings as the decision could take months.
If the three judges in the Court of Appeal choose to overturn her convictions, there are two options: a retrial or acquittal.
If the prosecution's appeal is successful, Erin Patterson could see her parole period being extended beyond 33 years. Or she may even be sentenced to life without parole.

One of the best things my smart home does is help me care for my pets, and security cameras are particularly useful for keeping track of my many critters. But the barrage of notifications they send often means I miss important ones. So, when Google announced its new Pet Memory feature for Gemini for Home, I thought this could be the perfect solution.
Google’s Pet Memory forgot who my cats are
Gemini for Home promises its Nest cameras can recognize my cats by name — but it can’t tell Boone from Smokey, making pet-focused smart notifications and automations mostly useless.
Google’s Pet Memory forgot who my cats are
Gemini for Home promises its Nest cameras can recognize my cats by name — but it can’t tell Boone from Smokey, making pet-focused smart notifications and automations mostly useless.
Pet Memory promises to teach your Google Home smart home who your pets are, allowing connected Nest cameras to go beyond simply telling you they saw an animal to which animal they saw. It can then use that knowledge to adapt your smart home to your pet.
My plan was to use it to keep a digital eye on my three cats while working in my home office, distinguish them from one another, and automate their feeding based on who was at the feeder. But after two weeks of testing, Google’s AI still can’t tell my three cats apart.
My house is on a suburban, three-quarter-acre lot in a quiet neighborhood, and I take full advantage of all this space to have as many animals as possible (my husband has already said no to a goat and horse). But I’ve managed to wrangle a flock of free-ranging chickens, a large, counter-surfing Wirehaired Pointing Griffon called Gus, two indoor/outdoor cats, and — most exciting of all — a new kitten.
As The Verge’s smart home reviewer, I test a lot of connected tech and have found my best use case for security cameras is monitoring my pets around my house and yard. They help keep the chickens safer from predators and my lunch safer from Gus, and act as a type of digital pet door for the cats. When I get a notification that there’s an animal at the door via a video doorbell and/or outdoor camera, it’s likely a cat wants to come in.
While I only have one dog and I don’t really need to distinguish the chickens by name, there were three things I thought Pet Memory could do to help me manage my three cats. First, identify which cat wanted in, and help prevent false alerts — such as when it’s my neighbor’s cat sitting on my porch, or when it’s a chicken peering in at the back door. Second, tell me whether all my pets were safely inside before dark. And finally, provide personalized automated feeding for each feline.
Recognizing individual pets is the latest step in a rapid evolution of smart security cameras. While some dedicated pet cams promise facial recognition, most standard security cameras could only alert you to motion until recently. Advances in machine learning and now generative AI are bringing more descriptive alerts. Instead of just announcing “motion alert,” cameras can increasingly tell you exactly what they saw, without you having to open the app and wait for a clip to load.
Nest has long been ahead of the game here, especially when it comes to critters. Its Nest Cam IQ, launched in 2017, could distinguish people from pets, and Google later brought animal detection to Nest cameras. More recently, Google added text descriptions that use AI to describe what the camera sees.
Amazon’s Ring, Wyze, and Apple Home (via its HomeKit Secure Video) have also recently added AI-powered descriptions, and these often include the type of animal detected (not always correctly). But Google Home is the first to personalize it.
However, there are limitations, and, of course, a cost. Pet Memory requires the top-tier Google Home Advanced Plan at $20 a month, and while it’s part of Google Home, it currently only works on Nest cameras. It also only works on indoor Nest Cams, so it wasn’t any use for my idea of an upgraded digital pet door.
I decided to set up a few indoor Nest Cams in strategic spots, hoping I could use Pet Memory to easily check which cats were inside. I thought it could help make sure everyone is safely home before dark. “Hey Google, when did you last see Smokey in the house?”
But despite telling Google Home what my three cats look like, it insisted they were all Smokey, the first cat I told it about. Asking the Google Nest Hub when Smokey was last spotted pulled up an adorable video of the new kitten playing in my daughter’s room.
From my testing, Pet Memory doesn’t appear to build an individual visual profile for each pet. There’s no training process, no opportunity to upload photos of my cats, and no way to correct mistakes. You enter a name and breed, and it tries to figure out the rest. I tried giving it more information — Boone is a tuxedo cat with white paws, Osa the kitten is a tabby cat, and Smokey is a large gray-and-white cat — but it said it couldn’t process the extra detail and kept labeling every cat as Smokey.
I asked Google why the system didn’t seem to be working as intended, but the company hasn’t responded with any details.
Still, I persisted in trying to get some use out of the feature, attempting to use Pet Memory to make my Aqara Pet Feeder smarter. I had previously set it up to trigger when Aqara’s G3 camera saw an animal, as it can’t identify species, let alone individuals.
But with a Nest Cam, I wanted to see if I could set it to dispense the right amount of food when it saw a specific cat — helping keep each from overeating without needing RF tags or other proprietary solutions smart pet feeders offer (my cats don’t do collars).
This was also an opportunity to try Google’s new ability to use camera detection events as triggers for automations and its Help Me Create feature, which can build an automation with just a description.
I typed what I wanted it to do into the Ask Home chatbot in the app. “Run my Aqara ‘Feed Smokey’ scene whenever the Nest Cam in the laundry room sees Smokey,” and it set it up for me. I then created a separate one for Boone. I ran into several issues.
The first — and biggest — was that it still couldn’t tell Boone from Smokey, so when either cat went to the feeder, it went off. The second problem is that the Google Home app doesn’t let you limit how many times an automation runs (something I could do with the Aqara automation). While the automation worked, it triggered every time either cat went to the bowl. By the end of one day, the food bowl was overflowing.
I also had high hopes for using Google’s Home Brief to get an overview of the critters’ day. This gives a rundown of activity from connected devices in your home at the end of the day. I told it I wanted more details about pet activity in my Home Brief, and now it mostly tells me “there were many pet interactions,” which isn’t helpful.
At one point, it told me Smokey was eating in the garage, which immediately raised a flag. Cats eating in the garage is never a good thing; there are too many things they shouldn’t be getting into. But when it showed me the relevant clip, it was Boone eating in the laundry room, as he should be.
I checked the garage camera, able to scroll back through the day’s footage, but neither cat was ever in there. Frankly, misidentification is worse than doing nothing at all. Getting the cat’s name wrong can be funny, but if you’re relying on it to tell you where your cats are, errors become consequential.
Recognizing individual pets turns out to be far harder than recognizing that there’s a pet at all. It’s a glimpse of where AI-powered cameras are headed, but not a feature I’d rely on today. AI has promised to cut down on the arduous work of searching through camera footage, but until it can reliably identify what happened, continuous recording is more useful than unreliable AI summaries.
Continuous recording is actually something Nest Cams do very well as part of that same $20 a month subscription. Whether it’s to keep an eye on your indoor kitten, a tropical aquarium, or a flock of chickens in your yard, scrolling back through a day’s worth of footage is invaluable when you’re trying to figure out what your cat ate that made them sick or how a chicken went missing (hawks don’t always trigger motion alerts). When AI can answer those questions for me, then it might be worth it; in the meantime, Boone is enjoying all the extra kibble.
