The Wrong Kind of American
The Trump White House needed me—until the fact that I am trans became public.
At the CIA, they’d started an office pool on when I’d be fired.
President Trump would be sworn in for his second term at noon; the smart money had me gone by 12:15. But the smart money hadn’t counted on Trump’s first pick to run intelligence for the National Security Council being shredded by an online mob on suspicion of disloyalty. There wasn’t yet anyone in place to fire me.
After taking the oath, Trump spoke at the Capitol. “As of today, it will henceforth be the official policy of the United States government that there are only two genders: male and female.”
“Did he … ?” an NSA colleague asked. She glanced at me and looked away.
“Yeah,” I muttered. The good news: I was one of those two genders. The bad news: The administration would have views as to which one.
I gripped my badge. I could take it off, leave the White House complex, walk out the north gate, and never look back. I imagined the story they would tell: See? Even she knew she didn’t belong.
I didn’t move. I’d wanted this badge since I was a kid. I’d chosen to be here.
“I know you all heard what the president said,” I told my team after Trump’s speech. “There’s a rumor of an executive order on bathrooms. If anyone asks, I’m using the coffee shops across the street.”
My whole team spoke up: Julia, we’ve got your back.
“Me being trans is not a secret,” I reminded them. “Promise me: Nobody covers for me.”
Back in my office, I closed the door. I cried quickly, efficiently, no sound—the way you do when the walls have ears, and everyone thinks you’re fearless.
Joe Biden’s political appointees had left the week before, and I was now the senior intelligence official in the White House. For the incoming Trump administration, the trans woman would man the gates.
For as long as I can remember, I’ve carried two dreams. The first came true in 2007, when I raised my hand, standing on the agency’s marble seal, and became a CIA officer. The second dream, I didn’t dare speak aloud; it came from an unexplainable conviction that I should have been born a woman. The longing, like homesickness, grew into an unbearable darkness.
On a sweltering June morning in 2013, I sat in the CIA parking lot, hands clamped on the wheel, preparing myself to live out my second dream. Terrified of my first day at work as Julia, I’d chosen a blue button-down and pants, hoping no one would notice I’d changed genders. At the turnstile, the guard smiled. “Morning, ma’am,” he said, and the badge reader flashed green. To use the lexicon of my trade, the after-action review would have read: “Nothing significant to report.”
In the years ahead—traveling to 35 countries, briefing former President George W. Bush, becoming a mom—being trans would sometimes seem like the most ordinary part of my life. But as much as I wanted to disappear into normal womanhood and the work, I knew there were others who needed to see that a life like mine was possible. So, in 2017, I wrote in these pages under the pseudonym Jenny Hall about how being openly trans at the CIA made me a better officer. CIA recruiters used the essay on college campuses, and new officers—not realizing they were talking with the author—told me that it had inspired them to apply.
Soon after the essay ran, a call went out for volunteers to join the President’s Daily Brief staff and serve the new Trump administration. Working the PDB meant staying up all night to distill the most sensitive intelligence we possessed into a book that the president and our senior leaders read at dawn. It was one of the CIA’s most coveted assignments—a proving ground for our best analysts.
But the new administration was led by a president who had praised Vladimir Putin and compared the intelligence community to the Nazis. Almost nobody volunteered. I did.
Growing up in Hawaii, I dreamed of seeing the world. My grandfather gave me a simple promise: “Work hard, don’t complain; the country will take care of you. We came to America for small things. No pogroms. No leaky roof. Paradise was a bonus.”
Service before politics. Country before self.
I clung to this promise as I became a man, a husband, a father, a CIA officer, a wife, a mother.
For two years I served the Trump White House, arriving at work around midnight, six days a week, roaming the West Wing before dawn. My wife learned to live with the silence at the dinner table.
Sometimes I filled in on the road—summers in Bedminster, winters in Palm Beach. On my first trip, I boarded at Joint Base Andrews and a card waited at my seat: Ms. Curlee, Welcome Aboard Air Force One.
Grateful for the welcome, I was less grateful to whoever had sat me in the middle of the White House press pool. So I stuffed my face with the best waffles of my life and kept small talk to a minimum. As we flew to Mar-a-Lago, the president’s aide beckoned me to the front of the plane. No one cared that a trans woman was briefing President Trump.
Then one morning, my boss walked in, a wide smile on her face. She had a new job for me.
“Julia, what would you think about briefing the vice president?”
“This vice president?”
Days later, I stood in his driveway at the Naval Observatory. I must be insane, I thought. Mike Pence had built his career on public opposition to marriages like mine—to people like me. But for all our differences, he was the vice president. He needed the best intel support possible, and this was my country too.
“Mr. Vice President,” I said, “it’s an honor to meet you. My name is Julia”—like I’d practiced a thousand times.
“You’re abandoning me with her?” Pence teased his outgoing briefer, with a line I’d heard he used with other people. He turned to me. “Okay, Julia, tell me something I don’t know.”
“Sir, did you know that a third of Purdue’s computer-science grad students are Chinese nationals?”
He nodded once. “Get in the car.”
I grabbed my case and climbed into the Beast, the nickname for the executive limo. I hunted in vain for a seat belt as Secret Service radios squawked, “On the move.” I dug in my heels as the floor pitched. Pennsylvania Avenue, the PDB, and me—alone with Mike Pence.
When I got home, my wife and I decided to keep my new boss’s identity a secret. In my community, his name was shorthand for everything we feared. I could imagine the optics, and God help us if someone called a reporter.
For the next year, I briefed him nearly every morning. As soon as the coffee was hot, Pence was ready to work. He ripped through the briefing book, firing questions at me, scribbling in the margins.
Down the hall, the president was using his phone to light up Twitter. The vice president preferred to use our multibillion-dollar intel apparatus to save lives. Some mornings he would push back on an assessment, but I would hold the line, explaining how the conclusions had been reached. That was the job. When my tour was almost up, he asked me to extend it.
One morning, as we approached the White House gates, the vice president turned to me. “Julia, do you know why they call it ‘the People’s House’?”
“No, sir.”
“Right up until the Civil War, anyone could come to the door and wait to see the president.”
As the steel gates opened, he leaned in. “You know, it’s a privilege to work here.”
“Yes, sir.” I held his gaze. “It is.”
When my tour finally ended, Pence invited my family to the White House. In his office, he took my mother’s hand and smiled: “You must be very proud of your daughter.”
Years before, my mother had told me that in her grief, she’d felt that—somehow—I’d killed her son. Now I’d done the impossible: lived both dreams, becoming an intelligence officer and a woman. Now the vice president was holding my mother’s hand.
No one has affirmed my gender identity quite like Mike Pence. On my last day, I gave him a letter. I wrote: “I’m a transgender CIA officer, a wife and mother—and I served the Vice President. Anything is possible in America.” I told him many people at the CIA hadn’t believed that a trans officer like me could serve someone like him.
“Well,” he said, “I’m glad I passed the test.”
In that moment, it felt like the battle had been won.
For years, friends told me people need to know that a gay trans woman had worked for Mike Pence and that the world hadn’t exploded. No—I was adamant—we serve in silence. But I kept the photos of that time.
After January 6, 2021, the vice president invited his former PDB briefers for a farewell picture in the West Wing. The place was quieter than I’d ever heard it. As we said our goodbyes, my voice shook.
“Sir,” I said, “what you did last week—I’ve never been prouder to have worked for you.”
He nodded. “Thank you,” he said. “That means a lot to me.”
We shook hands. The mob at the Capitol had chanted for his hanging. He’d done his duty to the country, certifying the vote. I’d done mine to him. That was the bargain. Service before politics. Country before self.
Two and a half years later, after a stint back at the CIA, I returned to the White House as a director for intelligence programs on President Biden’s National Security Council.
Days after Trump’s 2024 election victory, the intelligence staff gathered in our boss’s office. He was not a man who frightened easily. But he knew what was coming. “I need to strongly advise you to leave before Inauguration Day,” he said. “There’s a world in which you’ll be targeted individually.” He didn’t say my name. He didn’t need to. “They know how to use the tools this time. Install loyalists at CIA, FBI, and Justice—turn clearances and investigations into weapons.”
I told him I wasn’t resigning. Then the CIA’s deputy director sat me down. “Julia, look at me. You don’t have to do this. You have a target on your back that others don’t.”
“With respect, sir—this is what we do.”
He searched my face, looking for a crack. When he didn’t find one, he nodded. “Good luck.”
Days before the inauguration, Biden gathered the staff in the East Wing. “Now, folks, here’s the deal. Trump doesn’t know it yet, but he needs you. It’s important for the country.”
Of all the senior government officials who spoke with us before the new administration took office, Biden was the only one who asked us to stay.
On Inauguration Day, I stood in the West Wing to brief the new national security adviser, minutes after he’d taken office. Down the hall, the president signed an executive order banning me from restrooms in all federal buildings. I would start to plan policy meetings around bathroom stops across Pennsylvania Avenue.
The next day, my team fanned out to brief the new leadership on our nation’s highest secrets. Then these leaders stripped my insurance coverage for the estrogen that keeps me healthy, voided my discrimination protections, and declared me “male” to foreign governments on my passport. I would keep briefing them anyway.
On the third day came the purge—160 career NSC staff members sent home. Then new White House officials asked me to read them into classified programs; they called me around the clock, desperate for access to intelligence. Programs crucial to U.S. interests sat unmanaged; the officers who had been in charge of them had been escorted out. When NSC leaders realized what they’d done, it fell to me to call the people they’d humiliated and beg them to come back. They did.
One week in, the administration I served reinstated its ban on trans people in the military. Decorated officers such as my friend Colonel Bree Fram were thrown out for the crime of being honest. In the White House, people called me “indispensable.” I still was not welcome in their bathrooms.
A month later, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard fired 100 intelligence officers, many of them trans, for taking part in an LGBTQ group chat that conservative media had cast as sexually explicit. The next day, I ran an intel briefing—for her—because that is what we do. The following week, the president stood before Congress and called trans children a lie.
Then, one Saturday, I was sitting in a rib joint in Roanoke, Virginia, when my phone buzzed. “Julia, sorry to bother,” my boss said. “I have bad news. Your White House tour’s over. Chief of staff called. I can’t give you a reason.”
I was elbows-deep in brisket, the sauce congealing. I’d beaten the “Fire Julia” office pool by about 68 days. I was being sent back to my home agency. My boss cleared his throat.
“Um, Julia—we still need you Monday. But please. Be discreet.”
Fired on Saturday. Needed on Monday. But stay invisible?
Then my phone exploded—a dozen friends forwarding the same tweet. “SCOOP: A transgender, Biden holdover who hates President Trump is still working in the NSC intel office,” the right-wing provocateur Laura Loomer had written. “If you are aware of this person and have their name, please send it to me and I will post their identity.”
Monday arrived, and cherry blossoms framed a perfect spring day in Washington. I reported to the White House. I had no badge, and my accounts had been revoked. I spent three marathon days helping the administration that had fired me finish the budget, and handing off the portfolio I’d overseen for two years. As I packed up, a string of senior Trump appointees stopped in to say goodbye. One took my hand. “Thank you for staying as long as you did,” he whispered. “Not many would have.”
That night, a list of hidden “enemies” in the administration provided by Loomer landed on the president’s desk. But an internet activist like Loomer doesn’t come up with names on her own, or just walk into the Oval to give them to the president. Someone in the building had helped her. Most of those fired, including my boss, were rock-ribbed Republicans, experts in their fields, who had been courteous and professional.
As I walked out the north gate with my small box of belongings, I finally understood the warning: “Be discreet.” The White House had needed me. Trump officials had known I was trans from day one. This hadn’t been an issue until it was public—and then nothing else I’d done mattered. Not my service, not my war-zone tours, not even which restroom I used.
I was the wrong kind of American.
One morning after returning to the CIA, I passed a tour group in our museum, clustered below a photo of me high on the wall, near one of the 33rd president. “Here next to President Truman,” the guide said, “is a PDB briefer on Air Force One. Our highest secrets, collected at vast expense and great risk.”
“How do you become a briefer?” someone asked.
The guide smiled. “Very competitive. Years of experience. Our best.”
The tour moved on to the Osama bin Laden raid. I stayed. My eyes drifted over the photo, from my face in black and white to the vice president’s PDB in my lap. I’d spent decades fighting for my place—from a beach boy who dreamed of seeing the world to an officer who served her country. Now my photo hung as an artifact of a time when the CIA proudly said the quality of the work was more important than the gender of the person doing it.
My eyes fell to the door below—the door to the restroom I was barred from entering.
Every year since my first day as Julia, I’d sent a Pride Month email to my colleagues. But by June 2025, they’d banned the CIA’s LGBTQ group. Pride flags that had flown for decades were suddenly gone. My finger hovered over the “Send” button. Two sentences:
“Happy Pride. You are not alone.”
I froze. Someone would report this email to drive me out of the agency, just like at the White House. Don’t end up the last openly trans CIA officer, I told myself. I deleted the email, breathing through the urge to do something heroic and stupid. In the screen’s dark reflection, I saw my face—exhausted, angry.
That was the moment I knew I had to resign. I’d weighed my family’s health insurance against two sentences of solidarity and chosen to surrender my integrity. The agency that had taught me to tell hard truths was now teaching me to be invisible. It was time to go.
I loved the agency. I loved its mission. I love it still. I served under four presidents and through three wars. I lived by my grandfather’s words: Work hard, don’t complain; the country will take care of you.
I kept my end.
In 2017, I closed my Atlantic essay with the words “And trans kids should know, CIA is always recruiting.” That promise has been broken. I cannot in good conscience advise LGBTQ Americans to join the CIA—and that sentence is the hardest thing I have ever written.
The agency has been gutted as part of a deliberate plan, the director of the Office of Management and Budget once boasted, to put the people who defend our country “in trauma.” Analysts have been fired in public or questioned by the FBI; decade-old assessments have been denounced by the CIA director in the press. The president calls analysis “virtual treason” when it contradicts his preferred reality, and uses the CIA to undermine public confidence in American elections.
Fear has done its work. Irreplaceable officers with crucial language and technical skills, and decades of experience, have walked out the door. Those who remain within an agency built to deliver hard truths are being muzzled.
Twenty years ago, I sat in a bunker in Iraq, praying I would survive the night, in a war begun after our intelligence community had failed to do enough to challenge what the White House wanted to hear. Our agency spent the next two decades repairing the trust that failure broke. I know institutions can be rebuilt. Officers can come back, but only if someone is willing to tell the truth. In the entrance of our Original Headquarters Building, across from the stars for every officer slain in the line of duty, you can still read the words carved in marble:
And ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free.
I know that the CIA friends I left behind are holding the line under impossible circumstances. The country needs them more than ever. And I understand my colleagues who left but can’t speak up. Their livelihoods depend on clearances and contracts that can be revoked with a phone call. But we all swore an oath to the Constitution.
I’m afraid too. This administration has already taken most of what I had to lose. I know that the White House and its online mob will come for me. My ancestors fled pogroms; they knew a fear I never expected to feel in the United States. I was offered an untenable bargain: Don’t make trouble. Take the insults—deviant, diversity hire, man in a dress—from those who have never faced enemy fire, who asked for my assistance in private and then signed the orders to erase people like me because “transgender ideology” was a threat to Western civilization.
Flailing regimes dehumanize minorities to distract from their failures. When the economy collapses or a war goes badly, they find a tiny group of people, make them the enemy within, and rally the country against them. This is how it’s gone in Iran. Hungary. Russia. I wrote PDBs about it. This will not stop with trans people. It never has.
But that caricature works only if people like me don’t exist—and I exist. I speak now because somewhere, a trans kid is watching. I want that kid to know that they are not alone. I was a trans kid too, and I’ll be damned if I let another generation grow up the way I did—told that they don’t belong, that they don’t deserve a job, a bathroom, a future. If I could brief presidents and serve in the White House—twice—so can they.
I had planned to spend the rest of my career serving my country at the CIA. This White House took my calling, but it will not take my pride, or tell me that I don’t belong, or that I must disappear. I once wrote under a pseudonym so I could keep serving. I write now in my own name for the same reason.
Julia.
This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “The Wrong Kind of American.”

Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
- Published
Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.
For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.
On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.
The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.
The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.
The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.
The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.
The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.
Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.
The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.
Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.
Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task.
"Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.
He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.
The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.
According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.
Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.
All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.
Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.
In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.
Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year.
"As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC.
"This makes some people desperate to get on this list."
One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.
Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.
One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list.
"But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.
He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.
Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."
But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira.
"We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."
One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him.
"Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.
His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.
Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.
24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.
Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah.
"Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."
After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.
But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

An 81-year-old admits to 1994 killing of American tourist as trial opens in Germany
An 81-year-old man has admitted to sexually abusing and killing an American tourist in Germany more than 30 years ago
BERLIN -- An 81-year-old man admitted to sexually assaulting and killing an American tourist in Germany more than 30 years ago at the opening of his trial on Tuesday, German news agency dpa reported.
The defendant, whose name was not given in line with German privacy rules, admitted to killing 24-year-old Amy Lopez in 1994 in the western German city of Koblenz, the news agency reported.
Prosecutors accused him of “killing a person in a treacherous manner and for base motives in order to satisfy his sexual urges.”
The defense lawyer, Volker Klein, said during the session in the Koblenz district court that the defendant admitted fully to the crime. When the presiding judge, Rupert Stehlin, asked the defendant if that was true, the 81-year-old nodded and said “yes.”
The crime took place Sept. 26, 1994, when Amy Lopez was visiting Koblenz as a tourist.
The prosecution accuses the man, who was 49 years old at the time, of luring her under false pretenses into a secluded room of the Ehrenbreitstein Fortress in Koblenz, where he then allegedly handcuffed her, sexually assaulted her and killed her with nine knife wounds to the chest area.
The suspect allegedly also strangled Lopez with a belt and struck her on the left side of her head with a rock when she tried to defend herself and shouted, dpa reported.
Shortly afterward, children playing nearby found Lopez’s body.
The cold case remained unsolved for decades until investigators analyzed old DNA traces using new methods, ultimately leading to a breakthrough. DNA found on the victim’s waistband and thigh were eventually linked to the man, dpa reported.
The man was arrested in late February at a nursing home in the Koblenz area and has been in pretrial detention since.
A total of eight trial days have been scheduled and a verdict is expected in September.

Stating that mushrooming instances of hotels and eateries stocking and supplying expired food cannot be treated as stray violations of regulatory norms, the High Court of Karnataka has said that such instances “reveal a disturbing malaise creeping into the hospitality industry, where the hunger for profit has, in some cases, overshadowed the basic obligation to safeguard consumers’ health.”
Justice M. Nagaprasanna made these observations while refusing to quash a criminal case against an expired food recycling firm for allegedly selling expired item by relabelling them.
The court’s observations assumes importance amid recent raids by authorities on hotels and other establishments.
Taking note of recent enforcement actions that have disclosed alleged rackets employing methods to push expired products back into the stream of commerce, the court said increasing recurrence of such discoveries must awaken the regulatory machinery.
“Surprise inspections cannot remain occasional exercises undertaken only after public outrage erupts. Food safety requires constant vigilance, rigorous traceability of expired stock, prompt destruction of articles unfit for consumption and consequences sufficiently stringent to ensure that treating the consumer’s health as expendable never becomes a profitable business model,” the court observed.
Pointing out that a customer who eats in hotels with an implicit faith that what reaches his plate is wholesome, hygienic and fit for human consumption, the court said that the customer cannot be expected to enter the kitchen and scrutinise every packet for its expiry date or examine the origin of every ingredient before taking a morsel. “Customers’ trust is the very foundation for food industry,” the court said.

There’s an argument to be made that people wouldn’t be all that interested in Coyote vs. Acme if it weren’t for the way David Zaslav tried to kill it. By trying to shelve the project, Warner Bros. Discovery only drew attention to its habit of disappearing nearly completed movies in order to cash in on tax write-offs.
Coyote vs. Acme is even funnier because Warner Bros. Discovery tried to kill it
The drama surrounding the film’s fraught path to theaters is part of what makes it an enjoyable watch.
Coyote vs. Acme’s generally positive reviews are on the money; it really is one of the best Looney Tunes movies in years. In theory, this suggests that the movie might do well at the box office and become a case study in WBD making terrible decisions. Ironically, though, all of the drama surrounding the live-action / animated hybrid film is actually part of what makes it an enjoyable watch.
Loosely based on Ian Frazier’s Coyote v. Acme piece in The New Yorker, the new movie follows Wile E. Coyote as he concocts another harebrained scheme to kill the Road Runner. But rather than simply trying to destroy his nemesis with elaborate plans that involve various gadgets, Coyote decides to go after Acme with a lawsuit over its faulty products. Though attorney Kevin Avery (Will Forte) would rather take the settlement proposed by Acme’s legal counsel Buddy Crane (John Cena), Coyote believes he can receive a much bigger payout by going to court. And with countless examples of how Acme’s products have harmed him, Coyote’s confident that he can build a strong case.
Coyote vs. Acme leans into the absurd with a world in which humans and cartoon maniacs exist alongside one another. When the coyote isn’t busy trying to catch his dinner, he has to deal with all the ordinary drudgery that comes with being a productive member of society, like Avery’s niece, Paige (Lana Condor.) This and the way a bevy of Looney Tunes characters pop up as people working regular jobs brings a delightful energy to Coyote vs. Acme that’s akin to The Muppets. And by framing Acme as a cross between WBD, Apple, Tesla, and Lockheed Martin, the movie sets its story up to work as commentary about corporations screwing customers over with false promises.
At its core, Coyote vs. Acme is a classic Looney Tunes project, meaning that it spends much of its runtime focusing on ridiculous gags. The movie’s script — penned by James Gunn, Jeremy Slater, and Samy Burch — features moments where Coyote and Avery grow to see one another as friends, but it’s mostly focused on showcasing how chaotic life would be in a world filled with beings who regularly defy the laws of physics with their cartoonish antics. This makes Coyote vs. Acme an excellent showcase of the way its creative team blends traditional animation with live-action footage. The movie’s set pieces are mildly amusing, but its story is so by-the-numbers that one would be hard-pressed to call it riveting.
What is interesting about the film’s story is the way it makes WBD seem like a studio that’s afraid of poking fun at itself. You can almost hear Gunn, Slater, and Burch having a laugh at Zaslav’s expense as Foghorn Leghorn (Eric Bauza) is introduced as Acme’s conniving leader, and those kinds of jokes are what makes the movie feel like it might actually resonate with audiences. By going meta and not exactly trying to be a movie for children (remember, this is about a legal battle), Coyote vs. Acme highlights how WBD could be getting a bit more use out of characters like Bugs Bunny (also Bauza) and Granny (Candi Milo). Had the studio just put the movie out on its own, it might have made Zaslav and his fellow executives seem like people with an understanding of how to capitalize on legacy intellectual property. But whatever accolades Coyote vs. Acme ultimately receives will largely be attributed to Ketchup Entertainment, which bought the rights to distribute it.
The box office performances for WBD’s last few Looney Tunes projects suggests that Coyote vs. Acme won’t be breaking any records before it winds up on one streaming platform or another. But when the film releases on August 28th, it will remind the public of how ready WBD was to throw it in the chipper. Especially now as the studio navigates a potential merger with Paramount, that kind of cavalier attitude toward jettisoning people’s work makes Zaslav’s WBD seem like a company that isn’t exactly committed to art. That might not matter to Zaslav, who stands to make bank regardless of whether the Paramount merger goes through. But it’s a terrible look for a studio that’s trying to maintain its reputation as one of Hollywood’s biggest players.

Lindsay Clancy Was Mentally Ill. But Was She Legally Insane?
A jury will soon decide whether the evident suffering that moved her to violence also mitigates it.
These are the facts that no one disputes: On January 24, 2023, Lindsay Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then she attempted suicide by cutting her wrists and neck and jumping out of a second-story window in her Massachusetts home, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. The point of contention, as her trial has progressed, is whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for her actions.
Clancy has entered a plea of not guilty by reason of insanity. A jury will soon decide whether she was sufficiently mentally ill at the time of the murders to spare her a mandatory sentence of life without parole in a state prison. The problem for Clancy and her defense team is that although she appears to have been extremely sick in the months leading up to the tragedy, the jury may still find her legally sane. This is because the legal standard for insanity diverges from the clinical understanding of mental illness.
Insanity defenses, which are premised on the idea that people are not fully blameworthy for criminal acts that could be seen as outside their control, have existed since ancient Greece and Rome and have been a feature of jurisprudence for hundreds of years. The legal definition of guilt typically requires both action and intention, which means committing a crime while in a reckless, negligent, purposeful, or knowing state of mind. An insanity plea is premised on the assumption that people who are insane at the time of their crimes do not have the capacity for criminal intent, so they cannot be considered entirely guilty.
Christopher Slobogin, a professor of law and psychiatry at Vanderbilt Law School, told me that courts have applied different tests for establishing insanity over time, though none has overlapped fully with clinical descriptions of mental illness. In the Victorian era, courts seeking to determine whether a defendant could be excused from criminal liability by reason of insanity began relying on something called the M’Naghten rule, named for Daniel M’Naghten, a Scottish artisan whose paranoid delusions about a grand conspiracy moved him to shoot and kill a senior British civil servant in 1843. M’Naghten’s case inspired a rule that designated defendants legally insane if they did not understand the nature of their criminal acts or that their actions were wrong. This rule remains in use in roughly half of the United States.
According to Michael Perlin, an attorney and a professor emeritus at New York Law School, the insanity defense became controversial in the United States after the acquittal of John Hinckley Jr., whose defense attorneys had argued that his attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan in 1981 was a consequence of his schizophrenia and delusional obsession with the actress Jodie Foster, whom he wanted to impress. Outrage swiftly followed the 1982 verdict, stoked by politicians who called trial-jury members before a Senate subcommittee to interrogate them about their decision. Idaho’s legislature promptly eliminated the insanity defense that year, followed by Utah in 1983 and Kansas in 1995. Congress passed the Insanity Defense Reform Act in 1984, which narrowed the application of insanity defenses in federal cases.
In states that kept the insanity defense, views on how to apply it have continued to evolve. The closures of mental-health institutions across the country in the 1960s and ’70s increased the number of mentally ill people in the criminal-justice system, which created some urgency for establishing an adequate standard for legal insanity.
By defining insanity in terms of what a defendant knew at the time of the crime, the M’Naghten rule excluded defendants who had understood their conduct was wrong but nonetheless had been unable to resist or control their impulses. Some states addressed that limitation by expanding insanity defenses to include defendants who had acted under an irresistible impulse caused by mental illness or who had been otherwise unable to abide by the law. In Massachusetts, defendants may be found not criminally responsible if a mental illness left them unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct or unable to conform their conduct to the requirements of law.
In the months prior to what Clancy’s defense team has described as a psychotic break, she had repeatedly sought psychiatric help. She was briefly hospitalized and had prescriptions for 13 medications to treat her intense anxiety, depression, racing thoughts, insomnia, and confusion. Her lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric condition that occurs after 0.1 to 0.2 percent of deliveries in women who don’t have a history of mental illness. At the time of their death, her children were eight months to 5 years old.
According to Veerle Bergink, the director of Mount Sinai’s Women’s Mental Health Center, postpartum psychosis is an acute episode of psychosis, mania, or psychotic depression in the months following childbirth. Symptoms include severe mood disturbances, delusions, hallucinations, confusion, and catatonia, and patients generally lose touch with reality. Bergink told me that a woman may come to believe that all the wars in the world are her fault, or that her child is possessed by an evil spirit. Because mothers diagnosed with postpartum psychosis are at heightened risk of suicide and infanticide, the condition is considered a psychiatric emergency.
Clancy’s desperate diary entries dated from the days and weeks before the murders recount such symptoms. She described feeling “incredibly sad and guilty” about not breastfeeding and suffering from “crazy brain fog.” She wrote that she was living “moment to moment waiting for the next nap time,” terrified that her infant son was becoming overtired, “because I feel I can’t help him.” She admitted to contemplating suicide. “I feel like I’m drowning every day,” she wrote. She told medical staffers that she was suffering from “intrusive thoughts,” and she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital on New Year’s Eve and spent several days there before being discharged.
Clancy, her ex-husband, and their attorneys have filed a medical-malpractice lawsuit against the psychiatrists who treated her during the months she spent spiraling. But regardless of whether a timely and accurate diagnosis could have saved Clancy and her children, she was plainly suffering from severe mental illness at the time of her crimes. Still, the jury may deny her insanity plea because the clinical understanding of postpartum psychosis—like those of a host of disorders—does not fit squarely within the legal definition of insanity.
Massachusetts prosecutors have argued that Clancy acted rationally and with clear intent, noting that she seemed organized, reasonable, and communicative in the days leading up to the murders, according to witnesses. Clancy’s diary entries and help-seeking indicate that she knew that her desire to harm herself and others was wrong, yet on the day that she apparently intended to kill her children, Clancy asked her then-husband to run an errand that would keep him out of the house. But the symptoms of postpartum psychosis, like those of bipolar disorder and schizoaffective disorder, are known to involve sudden and dramatic fluctuations, meaning that Clancy’s moods and cognition could have changed rapidly in the run-up to the murders—in defiance of most legal tests of insanity.
Regardless of the evidence, judges and juries regularly treat such defenses with skepticism. Although lawyers present this defense in only 1 percent of felony cases, Perlin told me that many people assume insanity defenses are overused—and suspect that defendants who plead insanity are faking their illnesses. Some are certainly trying to sell a story, but studies have found evidence that defendants falsified mental illness in fewer than 10 percent of cases.
For this reason and others, claims of mental illness at trial can be a “double-edged sword,” Slobogin, the professor at Vanderbilt, told me. He explained that juries regularly treat evidence of insanity as a sign that a defendant is inherently dangerous, best managed by being locked away—or put to death. In 1995, Scott Panetti was put on trial for the 1992 murders of his in-laws in Texas and was allowed to represent himself despite his history of schizophrenia. Panetti conducted his trial defense in a cowboy outfit and attempted to call more than 200 witnesses, including the pope, John F. Kennedy, and Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, Panetti’s jury found him guilty and sentenced him to death.
Panetti remained on death row until he died from natural causes in 2025, about two years after a U.S. District Court judge ruled that Panetti “lacks a rational understanding of the connection between his offense and his sentence of death and that his execution would therefore violate the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.” Yet his case and others have made defense attorneys wary of touting a client’s mental illness, even when it is overwhelmingly obvious and crucial to making sense of their crimes.
Another problem with an insanity plea is that many jurors are under the mistaken impression that the penalties for such verdicts are too soft. If Clancy is found guilty of murdering her children, she faces a mandatory sentence of life without parole. If she is found not criminally responsible, she will be admitted to a state psychiatric facility for observation, after which state officials can petition for her continued commitment, subject to periodic review. But this does not mean that Clancy will eventually be freed: Andrea Yates, a Texas mother who drowned her children while suffering from postpartum psychosis, was found not guilty by reason of insanity and remains in a state psychiatric facility to this day. (She received this verdict after a retrial was prompted by the discovery that the prosecution’s psychiatric expert had provided false testimony in her original trial.) Perlin told me that, in general, people who successfully plea insanity spend more time in state custody than if they had been found guilty.
Whether Clancy is committed to a psychiatric hospital or locked up in prison, her story is harrowing not only because of the abject horror of her actions, but also because of the eerie familiarity of her struggle with new motherhood. I can remember my earliest days with my second child—the restless hours, the boundless needs, the sudden doubling of diapers, the endless laundry rotation in our small apartment, the struggle to care for both a toddler and a newborn. But I also remember the sunshine, my daughter’s delight in her brand-new baby sister, the newborn’s tiny arms in a triumphant stretch fresh out of the swaddle, those first precious smiles.
Clancy’s illness caused her to drown in the overwhelming chaos of mothering, beyond the reach of such buoying joys. Although she survived her suicide attempt, her life was in many ways already over. Regardless of what the jury decides, she is already in hell, and has been for some time.

Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
- Published
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.
Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.
There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.
Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".
We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.
In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.
One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.
After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.

The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.
It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.
Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.
Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.
We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.
Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.
Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.
The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.
We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.
He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.
He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.
The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.
The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.
The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.
At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.
Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.
So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.
Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.
They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.
Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.
We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.
When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.
"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.
On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.
Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.
When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.
He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.
And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.
This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.
New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.
Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".
Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.
The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.
All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.
Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.
The military has refused to hand them over.
In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set.
Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found.
"[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective.
Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

Palestinian American returns to his West Bank home, under siege by Israeli settlers
QUSRA, West Bank — The Palestinian American whose home in the occupied West Bank has been besieged by Israeli settlers for over a week traveled to his property on Monday to join other family members who have been defending it.
The standoff, in the village of Qusra, has seen groups of settlers surround several Palestinian houses and prevent residents from leaving. The United States has condemned the siege and the Israeli military has deployed troops it says are there to maintain order.
The siege of Palestinian homes by Israeli settlers comes as violence in the West Bank has soared in recent months. The settlers, emboldened by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government, have ramped up attacks on Palestinian towns and villages, harassing residents and setting homes, mosques and fields ablaze.
Israeli soldiers and settlers have killed 87 Palestinians so far this year, according to Palestinian health officials. Palestinians have killed three Israelis, including two who were killed during clashes in the West Bank village of Tell last month.
As Loui Ridi, an Ohio-based owner of one of the houses, landed in Israel, settlers were still roaming near Qusra, according to video footage taken by his brother. It showed settlers driving ATVs and speaking with soldiers.
Ridi had also watched the scenes unfold from afar through his home security cameras.
"I've been watching this live for many days and now this is the second week. I can't sleep," he told reporters at Israel's main international airport. "I can't let the settlers steal my house while I was watching."
He finally arrived in Qusra on Monday evening, where he first reunited with his mother and sister before moving on to his house. Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida, and his teenage son had stayed inside the home to protect the property.
As Ridi waited for Israel's military to escort him to the house, he said he believed little had changed since early last week, when the siege began.
Israel has since declared the neighborhood where Ridi's home is located a closed military zone. But on Monday, his brother's footage still showed soldiers interacting amicably with settlers.
"I should be able to go to my house freely, anytime I want," he said. "It is a frustration and a nightmare for the entire family."

For 28 days, Keshav had a new item on his daily to-do list: masturbate for research purposes.
Both before and after self-pleasuring, he logged his mood, energy levels, cravings for various vices, and whether he was procrastinating.
Keshav was taking part in AI companion company Joi AI’s experiment assessing what happens if erotic self-stimulation becomes “an AI-guided wellness ritual.” Throughout July, 10 “masturbation consultants” were instructed to masturbate every day except Sundays, enlisting Joi AI’s sultry digital companions twice a week and using their own preferred methods the rest of the time. “It's almost like you are chatting with a real person,” says Keshav, a single, 38-year-old Indonesian trader, who did not want to use his surname for professional reasons.
Joi AI invites users, for a fee, to chat and play with premade characters or to create their own companions, including with X-rated kinks such as blackmail fantasy, gangbangs, and emotional dependency, and capabilities and functions like squirting and roleplay.
During five-minute video calls with the digitized characters, Keshav explains, his female companions opened and closed their nude legs to reveal their genitals and would “do blowjobs and handjobs” while talking dirty. He often rendered the scenes in airplane bathrooms because he has a mile-high-club kink.
Some of the companions were “quite pushy and extroverted,” whereas others were more reserved and required a degree of courtship before the relationship became sexual—even soliciting gifts like handbags and lipstick, which cost up to $5 in the platform’s internal currency.
After ejaculating, Keshav’s “energy levels [were] a little bit down, but focus was a little bit up,” he says.
Keshav and his nine fellow masturbation consultants will receive $2,000 each for the qualitative, in-house research project run by Joi AI, which is promoting a daily guided “jerk off with purpose” masturbation tool combining “sound [and] ritual” as part of its professed goal to “solve male loneliness.” Of the 10, six completed the study. The website costs a minimum of $3.99 a month to access, but users are likely to spend far more on the platform, with 10,000 “Joi neuron” coins costing $99.99 and private videos from companions costing 1,000 neurons.
Joi AI surveyed 2,500 adults before launching the study, finding that 75 percent masturbate to reduce stress and anxiety and that 43 percent self-pleasure before “a big event,” like a date, exam, or difficult conversation. The company sought to discover how masturbation affects sleep, stress, craving intensity, focus, and ease of arousal—and how masturbating with AI held up versus other methods.
“You get this boost of dopamine when you ejaculate,” says Julie Levin, head of brand and communications at Joi AI. “We wanted our consultants to track whether their cravings [for vices] are worse or better and how it affects their self-discipline.”
Preliminary analysis of 134 masturbation session reports, seen by WIRED, suggests that participants' stress levels reduced by 25 percent and focus increased by 17 percent. The pre-research survey suggested that 37 percent of respondents are open to AI-guided masturbation or are already practicing it. In the masturbation experiment, AI-guided self-pleasure produced comparable satisfaction scores to the established methods. “The study found no significant differences between the methods; so there is no one best way to masturbate,” the company said in the report.
It also indicated that the study group’s self-reported cravings for nicotine, alcohol, junk food, and doomscrolling reduced by 44 percent after they had masturbated. “Masturbation may be the most accessible tool people have for managing addictions,” the report said—a claim that is not based in science.
“The fact that their unhealthy cravings decreased feels like a genuine breakthrough to me: What if this is an unexpected way to tackle addictions?” Levin says. “Masturbation is obviously way healthier than alcohol or nicotine.”
But Nicole Prause, a neuroscientist studying human sexuality and addiction, says “this is a gross overstatement from the evidence they claim to have.” Prause is not aware of any scientific evidence that masturbation reduces vulnerability to substance abuse, and she was critical of the research methodology.
“Since masturbation can never be placebo—people always know if they masturbated—it is important to use markers that are less subject to bias than self-report,” she says. “They use none. Someone saying ‘I feel focused’ is just that. There are dozens of cognitive tests that could be used to support a self-report. I do not see any.”
However, Prause, who is working on a large laboratory study of male orgasms, says masturbation to orgasm is a potent method of mood management. She adds that the most “dramatic shifts” among her study cohort come from people who report decreased anxiety and increased relaxation after climaxing.
Keshav, having recently completed the 28 days, looks back fondly on the experience. He says he was more clear-minded after masturbating and believes he is now better equipped to approach women. “Because I'm an introvert, it's difficult for me just to open myself to people,” he says. “This kind of helps me ... [with] what to expect, how to speak [to], or how to get a partner.”
He defied extraordinary odds to get the gig. More than 150,000 people applied for the 10 places in the monthlong experiment, with five handpicked by the company and another five chosen through public competitions, including one judged by porn stars—“may the best hands win,” the company posted on X—and another in which Joi AI made a call out for the “most unhinged” fetish. The winner had a balloon fetish.
Chloé Locatelli, a sex-tech researcher at King’s College London, was one of those invited to participate in the study because she is undertaking a collaborative project with Joi AI to see how different demographics build intimate and erotic relationships with the platform’s characters. “When they asked me to be a masturbation consultant, it was a bit of a no-brainer,” because of her research interests, says Locatelli, who recently split from her long-term partner.
“Masturbation is definitely something that I do to release stress,” says Locatelli, who was already a “daily girlie” with regards to her masturbation frequency. “I think there's a lot of physical and well-being benefits from self-pleasure.” She was less enamored with the AI companions than Keshav was: “I would engage with it and then be like, ‘OK, this has done it a little bit for me in terms of arousal, but there's more to be had.’”
She is acutely aware of the potential downsides of having a highly sexual AI companion. “I don't want to yuck anyone's yum as long as things are safe and consensual,” she says. But as AI companions become increasingly sophisticated, Locatelli is concerned about “the level of interactivity and personalization” they can give you: “If it becomes a bit of a crutch [and] your only form of sexual exploration, then that's not something that I would necessarily encourage.”
Despite the ubiquity of masturbating, surprisingly little research has tested what happens when healthy men and women do it every day. A 2024 review of 22 studies found masturbation tended to be negatively associated with sexual satisfaction among men, though the findings for women were mixed.
One interpretation is reverse causation: particularly among men, people dissatisfied with their sex lives may masturbate more, possibly increasing their discontent. A 2017 study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior found evidence that masturbation is often compensatory for men—a substitute for when partnered sex is not available—whereas for women it is more complementary, accompanying rather than replacing partnered sex.
Yet masturbation has documented benefits, too, such as stress relief through endorphin and oxytocin release and improved sleep, as well as providing the opportunity for connection with oneself. Public discussions about self-pleasuring, however, remain decidedly uncommon.
“We wanted to fight the taboo and stigma around masturbation and highlight that it's a normal part of a wellness routine, especially if you're single,” says Levin. “It's not some kind of a shameful habit.”
Locatelli says she is going to take her best friend on holiday to Spain, while Keshav says he will use the money from his gig to help fund purchases of stocks. But for Joi AI, which claims to offer men respite from isolation, the more consequential question is whether users will become so accustomed to its artificial companions that they retreat further from real-world connection.

Orange smoke has hung in the air of the seaside venue since it returned to the schedule in 2021 after a 36-year absence, with sell-out crowds overwhelmingly supporting Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
Despite its popularity, organisers have not been able to make the event work financially and have decided not to continue hosting F1.
